A small freely falling cloud can stretch along one axis and shrink along another. The full Riemann tensor keeps track of those directional tidal changes. A contraction combines some of that information, rather as a matrix trace combines its diagonal entries.

The resulting Ricci tensor is especially useful for the volume behaviour of a geodesic cloud. Its contraction with the cloud's velocity enters the focusing equation. But it cannot retain every shape distortion: radial stretching can be balanced by transverse squeezing, leaving a vanishing Ricci tensor while tides remain.

So Ricci is a useful summary of curvature, not another name for all curvature. This distinction is essential when we later impose vacuum field equations.
statement: Ricci curvature contracts Riemann’s directional information into a tensor that helps govern volume focusing.

title: Contract a specific pair
body: With the atlas curvature convention, define \[R_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq R^\rho{}_{\mu\rho\nu}.\] The summed index is the first upper and third lower slot of Riemann as written. For the Levi-Civita connection the result is symmetric, so it has ten independent components in four dimensions.
statement: Our Ricci tensor is the contraction \(R_{\mu\nu}=R^\rho{}_{\mu\rho\nu}\).

title: Volume change versus shape change
body:
An initially comoving small cloud can stretch in one direction while shrinking in another. The trace of its tidal acceleration involves \(R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\), while directional distortions require more of Riemann. For an initially nonexpanding, shear-free, rotation-free timelike geodesic bundle, the initial expansion rate obeys \(d	heta/d	au=-R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\). In general shear, rotation and existing expansion also contribute.

\explanation{trace-tides}{What information does the trace lose?}{At the initial instant, the weak-field point-mass tidal matrix has eigenvalues proportional to \((2,-1,-1)\). Their sum is zero, but none is zero individually. The cloud begins to change shape without a first-order trace acceleration. Later shear can also affect its volume, so zero Ricci does not guarantee constant volume throughout its evolution.}
statement: Ricci contraction controls one contribution to geodesic-cloud focusing; expansion, shear and rotation also matter.

title: Vacuum can still produce tides
body: Outside an isolated spherical mass, with zero cosmological constant, \(R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0\). Nevertheless a falling cloud stretches radially and contracts transversely. The remaining trace-free part of Riemann, called Weyl curvature, carries this tidal information. Ricci-flat therefore does not mean flat.
statement: A Ricci-flat vacuum can retain trace-free Weyl curvature and measurable tides.

title: What further contractions retain
body: Contracting Ricci with the inverse metric gives the \cref{Ricci scalar}{gr.ricci_scalar}. Combining that scalar with Ricci gives the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor}. Each contraction discards information; none is an interchangeable name for the full curvature tensor.
statement: Taking further traces reduces curvature information; Ricci, scalar curvature and Einstein curvature are distinct objects.

title: A scalar from curvature
body: The Ricci scalar assigns a coordinate-independent number to each event by tracing the Ricci tensor with the metric. It is compact enough to serve as a gravitational action integrand, but contains much less information than either Ricci or Riemann.
statement: The metric trace of Ricci gives a coordinate-independent scalar but discards further curvature information.

title: A metric trace
body: Define \[R\coloneqq g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}.\] This is a tensor contraction, not the ordinary sum of diagonal entries in an arbitrary chart. In a local orthonormal frame of signature \(+---\), it reads \(R\overset{\text{orthonormal frame}}{=}R_{\hat0\hat0}-R_{\hat1\hat1}-R_{\hat2\hat2}-R_{\hat3\hat3}\). The hats denote frame components rather than coordinate labels.
statement: Scalar curvature is \(R=g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}\), a metric trace rather than a plain coordinate diagonal sum.

title: Curvature proportional to the metric
body:
If a four-dimensional geometry has \(R_{\mu
u}=A g_{\mu
u}\), where \(A\) is a scalar, then \[R\overset{	ext{given Ricci}}{=}A g^{\mu
u}g_{\mu
u}=4A.\] The factor four counts dimensions; signature does not change the trace of the identity. In \(n\) dimensions this example gives \(nA\).
statement: If \(R_{\mu\nu}=A g_{\mu\nu}\) in four dimensions, then \(R=4A\).

title: Cancellation loses information
body: A vanishing trace can hide nonzero Ricci components, and even zero Ricci can hide Weyl curvature. Thus \(R=0\) alone establishes neither vacuum nor flatness. Its sign also depends on the chosen curvature and metric conventions; it is not a convention-free label for attractive or repulsive gravity.
statement: Vanishing scalar curvature establishes neither vacuum nor flatness.

title: From scalar to action
body:
The product \(R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x\) is an invariant integration density. Its integral enters the \cref{Einstein-Hilbert action}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action}, whose variation contains the full Ricci tensor rather than only the scalar. With length-valued coordinates, \(R\) has dimensions of inverse length squared.

The two ingredients solve different problems. Contracting with the \cref{inverse metric}{gr.inverse_metric.definition} removes the remaining Ricci indices and produces a scalar. Multiplying by the \cref{volume density}{gr.volume_element.why_needed} then makes its integral independent of coordinate labels. The scalar alone is not a coordinate integration measure.
statement: Combining scalar curvature with invariant four-volume gives the Einstein–Hilbert action integrand.

title: A divergence-free curvature combination
body: Ricci alone generally has a nonzero covariant divergence. Subtracting half its metric trace produces the Einstein tensor, whose divergence vanishes identically. This makes it compatible with a locally conserved stress-energy source.
statement: Subtracting half the metric trace from Ricci gives an identically divergence-free curvature tensor.

title: Subtract the trace term
body:
Define \[G_{\mu
u}\coloneqq R_{\mu
u}-	frac12 Rg_{\mu
u}.\] It is symmetric for the Levi-Civita connection and depends on the metric and its derivatives through second order. The symbol \(G_{\mu
u}\) denotes a tensor; the unindexed constant \(G\) denotes Newton's gravitational constant.
statement:
The Einstein tensor is \(G_{\mu
u}=R_{\mu
u}-	frac12 Rg_{\mu
u}\).

title: Why one half appears
body:
Combine \cref{Ricci curvature}{gr.ricci_tensor.definition} with its \cref{metric trace}{gr.ricci_scalar.definition}. Consider the family \(H_{\mu
u}=R_{\mu
u}-aRg_{\mu
u}\), with constant \(a\). The contracted Bianchi identity supplies
\[
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}=	frac12
abla_
u R.\]
Metric compatibility then gives
\[
abla^\mu H_{\mu
u}=(	frac12-a)
abla_
u R.\]
Thus \(a=1/2\) makes this combination divergence-free for every smooth metric with its Levi-Civita connection, not only for solutions of Einstein's equations.

This cancellation is why the trace term matters. It constructs a geometric tensor whose divergence can match the local covariant conservation law for matter. It does not yet establish a physical field equation.
statement: The contracted Bianchi identity fixes the factor one-half needed to cancel the divergence.

title: The trace in four dimensions
body: Tracing the definition gives \[G^\mu{}_{\mu}=R-\tfrac12(4)R=-R.\] Consequently \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\) implies \(R=0\) and then \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) in four dimensions. This argument changes with dimension; in two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.
statement: In four dimensions the Einstein tensor has trace \(-R\); its vanishing then implies Ricci flatness.

title: An identity does not determine gravity
body:
The divergence identity neither sets \(G_{\mu
u}\) to zero nor identifies it with matter. That additional physical relation is the \cref{Einstein field equation}{gr.einstein_field_equations}. A constant multiple of the metric also has zero divergence, allowing a cosmological term. Divergence-free is weaker than covariantly constant: \(
abla_ho G_{\mu
u}\) need not vanish.
statement: A divergence identity constrains a possible field equation but does not by itself supply one.

title: Curvature has internal consistency
body: Curvature is built from a connection rather than specified independently at each event. Its derivatives therefore satisfy identities. The differential Bianchi identity is the one that makes the Einstein tensor's divergence vanish.
statement: Curvature built from a connection obeys differential consistency identities before any field equations are imposed.

title: A cyclic differential identity
body:
For the Levi-Civita connection the differential Bianchi identity is
\[ egin{aligned}0&\equiv
abla_\lambda R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}\ &\quad+
abla_\mu R^ho{}_{\sigma
u\lambda}\ &\quad+
abla_
u R^ho{}_{\sigma\lambda\mu}.\end{aligned}\]
The sum cycles \(\lambda,\mu,
u\): one derivative direction and the last two curvature directions. This is a geometric identity satisfied by curvature, rather than a matter equation or a restriction imposed only on physical solutions. The algebraic Bianchi identity instead cycles three curvature slots without differentiating.
statement: The cyclic covariant derivative of Riemann over its derivative and antisymmetric curvature slots vanishes.

title: Why an identity exists
body:
At any regular event choose normal coordinates, so \(\Gamma=0\) at that event. The curvature formula reduces there to the difference of two first derivatives of \(\Gamma\). In its derivative, the differentiated quadratic products still vanish at that event because each contains a factor of \(\Gamma\).

In the cyclic derivative sum, terms such as \(\partial_\lambda\partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma}\) cancel with the same mixed derivative in the opposite order. Smoothness allows those ordinary derivatives to commute. The entire cyclic sum is therefore zero at the event.

Because the final statement is a tensor identity, checking it in normal coordinates establishes it in every regular chart. The event was arbitrary, so the identity holds throughout the smooth region. No gravitational field equation was used.
statement: In normal coordinates, commuting second derivatives of connection coefficients cancel in the cyclic sum.

title: Contract to a useful form
body:
Contracting with the metric and using Riemann's symmetries produces \[2
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-
abla_
u R\equiv0.\] By the definition of the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and metric compatibility this becomes \(
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\equiv0\). The contraction hides much of the original index structure while retaining the identity needed for source consistency.

\explanation{contracted-bianchi}{Follow the two contractions}{Write the cyclic identity with all curvature indices lowered, and contract the derivative index against one curvature index and a second pair using the inverse metric. Metric compatibility lets both inverse metrics pass through the derivatives. Riemann's pair symmetries turn the two surviving Ricci derivatives into the same \(
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}\), while the scalar-trace term has the opposite sign. Their sum is \(2
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-
abla_
u R=0\).}
statement:
Contracting the differential identity gives \(2
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}=
abla_
u R\).

title: Geometry and matter play different roles
body:
For constant \(\Lambda\), both \(G_{\mu
u}\) and \(\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\) are divergence-free. Applying the field equation then requires \(
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}=0\). This is a compatibility statement about a coupled solution; the geometric identity alone is not a matter equation of motion or a guarantee of a globally conserved total energy.
statement: The geometric identity requires source consistency in a coupled solution, but does not imply a global conserved energy.

title: Test geometry rather than chart components
body: A component can diverge because coordinates fail. Scalar contractions of curvature take the same value at an event in every regular chart, so their divergence is stronger evidence of a geometric problem.
statement: Scalar curvature contractions help distinguish coordinate divergences from invariant curvature growth.

title: Useful contractions
body:
Common examples are the Ricci scalar \(R\), the squared Ricci contraction \(R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u}\), and the Kretschmann scalar \[K\coloneqq R_{\mu
uho\sigma}R^{\mu
uho\sigma}.\] All indices are contracted with the metric. Despite the language of a square, such Lorentzian contractions need not be positive for arbitrary tensors or geometries.
statement: Complete contractions such as \(R\), \(R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}\) and the Kretschmann scalar are coordinate-invariant.

title: Schwarzschild separates two suspect radii
body:
For Schwarzschild geometry define the mass length \(m=GM/c^2\). Evaluating its curvature gives
\[\begin{aligned}R&=0,\\ K&=\frac{48m^2}{r^6}.\end{aligned}\]
At \(r=2m\), substitution gives \(K=3/(4m^4)\), which is finite for any positive mass. At \(r\to0\), however, the same scalar diverges.

This comparison is stronger than inspecting a metric component: every regular coordinate chart assigns the same value to \(K\) at the event. A chart extension removes the horizon's component divergence, whereas it cannot remove the central divergence of this scalar. The result also illustrates why \(R=0\) alone misses important curvature.
statement: Schwarzschild has finite Kretschmann curvature at its horizon but divergent curvature as \(r\to0\).

title: Check dimensions and scale
body: Since curvature has dimensions of inverse length squared, \(K\) has dimensions of inverse length to the fourth power. Doubling \(r\) at fixed mass reduces Schwarzschild's \(K\) by 64. This quantifies local curvature, not the strength of a coordinate acceleration or the existence of a horizon.
statement: Curvature has inverse-length-squared dimensions; the Kretschmann scalar has inverse-length-to-the-fourth dimensions.

title: A diagnostic is not a complete regularity theorem
body: Finite scalar invariants do not prove extendibility or geodesic completeness, and some curved Lorentzian geometries have vanishing polynomial curvature invariants. A complete singularity analysis examines causal geodesics and possible extensions. See \cref{coordinate singularity}{gr.coordinate_singularity} and \cref{black-hole singularity}{gr.black_hole_singularity} for the Schwarzschild distinction.
statement: Finite or vanishing scalar invariants alone do not establish flatness, completeness or extendibility.

title: Let the metric be dynamical
body:
A particle action asks which path a test body follows in a prescribed metric. A gravitational action asks which metric field is physically allowed. The unknowns are now the functions \(g_{\mu\nu}(x)\), so a variation changes clocks, rulers and curvature throughout a region.

The \cref{Ricci scalar}{gr.ricci_scalar} provides a scalar built from that metric and its first two derivatives. The \cref{invariant volume element}{gr.volume_element.definition} allows us to integrate it without privileging a coordinate grid. Their combination gives the Einstein–Hilbert action, the simplest curvature action used in GR.

Matter contributes its own action. Stationarity of the combined action then relates geometry to the metric response of matter, rather than obtaining dynamics from geometry alone.
statement: Varying a gravitational action changes the metric itself, rather than a particle path on a fixed geometry.

title: Keep action and curvature signs together
body: Use \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G\), signature \(+---\), and the atlas Riemann convention. Define \[S_g\coloneqq-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(R+2\Lambda).\] This pairs with \(\delta S_m=\tfrac12\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}\). Other consistent conventions use different signs; copying the action alone from them changes the theory's relative coupling.
statement: In our conventions and \(c=1\), \(S_g=-(2\kappa)^{-1}\int dV_4(R+2\Lambda)\).

title: Two variations make the Einstein tensor
body:
Use \(c=1\), \(\kappa=8\pi G\), and vary the inverse metric. Write \(h^{\mu
u}\coloneqq\delta g^{\mu
u}\). The determinant and curvature variations are
\[ egin{aligned}\delta\sqrt{-g}&=-	frac12\sqrt{-g}\,g_{\mu
u}h^{\mu
u},\ \delta R&=R_{\mu
u}h^{\mu
u}+g^{\mu
u}\delta R_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
For the Levi-Civita connection, the last contracted term is a divergence. Restricting to compactly supported variations removes its integral. The remaining contributions to \(\delta S_g\) are therefore the Ricci term, the determinant's trace term and the cosmological term.

Writing \(E_{\mu
u}\coloneqq G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\), their combination is
\[\delta S_g=- rac1{2\kappa}\int dV_4\,E_{\mu
u}h^{\mu
u}.\]
The half-trace in \(G_{\mu
u}\) comes from varying the volume element. Keeping only the explicit \(R_{\mu
u}h^{\mu
u}\) contribution would miss it.

\explanation{determinant-variation}{Why does inverse-metric variation give a minus sign?}{The determinant identity gives \(\delta\ln|g|=g^{\mu
u}\delta g_{\mu
u}\). Differentiating \(g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha
u}=\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\) then gives \(\delta g_{\mu
u}=-g_{\mu\alpha}g_{
u eta}\delta g^{\alpha eta}\). Taking half the logarithmic determinant variation produces the displayed negative sign.}

\explanation{palatini-divergence}{Why is the remaining curvature variation a divergence?}{The difference of two connections is a tensor, so \(\delta\Gamma\) is tensorial. For the atlas curvature convention,
\[\delta R_{\mu
u}=
abla_ho\delta\Gamma^ho{}_{
u\mu}-
abla_
u\delta\Gamma^ho{}_{ho\mu}.\]
Contract with \(g^{\mu
u}\). Since \(
abla g=0\), the inverse metric can be moved inside each derivative, leaving a covariant divergence. The divergence theorem converts its volume integral to a boundary term.}
statement: Varying scalar curvature and invariant volume together produces the Einstein tensor in the interior variation.

title: Stationarity supplies the field equation
body:
Adding the matter variation and requiring \(\delta(S_g+S_m)\overset{	ext{stationary}}{=}0\) for arbitrary interior metric variations yields \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The gravitational action selects dynamics; the Bianchi identity checks their consistency. See \cref{stress-energy variation}{gr.stress_energy_variation} for the source definition.

\explanation{arbitrary-variation}{Why must the tensor coefficient vanish?}{After adding the matter term, the integrand is proportional to \((-E_{\mu
u}+\kappa T_{\mu
u})h^{\mu
u}\). Each independent symmetric component of \(h^{\mu
u}\) may be chosen arbitrarily within a small interior region. If its coefficient were nonzero there, some allowed variation would make the action change to first order. Stationarity for all such choices therefore sets that coefficient to zero.}
statement:
Combining gravitational and matter variations yields \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}\).

title: Boundary conditions are part of the problem
body: Compactly supported variations justify the local derivation above. On a region with a boundary, fixing only the induced metric does not generally remove the normal derivatives of its variation from the bare action. A suitable gravitational boundary term is then required. The cosmological term is optional physics, while the boundary treatment is necessary for the stated variational problem.
statement: Compact interior variations remove boundary terms; fixing an induced boundary metric generally requires an added gravitational boundary action.

title: The local source of curvature
body:
Rest mass is only part of what matters gravitationally. A beam of light carries energy and momentum; a compressed fluid also carries pressure. The stress-energy tensor packages these contributions into one object that all observers can describe consistently.

Its role is local: at an event, an observer resolves the tensor into measured energy density, energy flow, momentum density and stress. Another observer can obtain different component values while agreeing about the underlying tensor.

GR couples this tensor to the spacetime metric. The \cref{SR energy–momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} supplies the flat-spacetime interpretation; here the measuring frames and comparison rules belong to a curved geometry.
statement: Matter and nongravitational fields source gravity through their local energy, momentum and stress.

title: What an observer measures
body:
For an observer with four-velocity \(v\), normalised by \(g(v,v)=c^2\), define the measured energy density \[\epsilon_{(v)}\coloneqq rac{1}{c^2}T_{\mu
u}v^\mu v^
u.\] This contraction is a scalar once the observer is specified. Different observers can measure different densities at the same event without disagreeing about the tensor.

Here \(T_{\mu
u}\) is the symmetric physical stress-energy tensor of the matter and nongravitational fields, rather than an arbitrary rank-two tensor. Specifying the observer is essential: invariance under changing coordinates does not mean every moving observer measures the same energy density.
statement: Stress-energy is the symmetric rank-two local energy–momentum source; an observer measures \(T(v,v)/c^2\) as energy density.

title: Components in a local rest frame
body:
Use an observer's local orthonormal frame, with time coordinate \(x^{\hat0}=ct\), and the balance convention \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\). The second index labels the energy or momentum being carried; the first labels the flow direction.

Then \(T^{\hat0\hat0}\) is energy density, \(cT^{\hat i\hat0}\) is energy flux, \(T^{\hat0\hat i}/c\) is momentum density and \(T^{\hat i\hat j}\) is momentum flux or stress. Symmetry relates energy flux to momentum density by the familiar factor \(c^2\).

\explanation{pressure-flux}{Why is pressure a momentum flux?}{Molecules reflecting from a wall transfer momentum to it even when the gas has no net bulk motion. Pressure measures that transfer per unit area and time. This is why a fluid at rest can have nonzero spatial stress components.}

Arbitrary coordinate components need not equal these instrument readings: the coordinate basis may not consist of unit orthogonal rods and a unit clock direction.
statement: Orthonormal components distinguish energy density, energy flux, momentum density and stress.

title: More than rest mass gravitates
body: Pressure, radiation and field energy all contribute to \(T_{\mu\nu}\). A \cref{perfect fluid}{gr.perfect_fluid} provides a simple model, while \cref{metric variation of matter}{gr.stress_energy_variation} supplies a general construction. The source includes all interacting matter sectors together; one sector may exchange energy with another.
statement: Pressure, radiation and field energy contribute to the gravitational source alongside rest mass.

title: Do not add a local gravity tensor by analogy
body: The right-hand source in Einstein's equation is not a general local tensor density of gravitational energy. Gravitational dynamics also reside in the metric's nonlinear field equation. Accordingly \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation} does not by itself provide a conserved total energy for every spacetime.
statement: The matter source is not a universal local tensor of gravitational-field energy.

title: Isotropy defines the idealisation
body: A perfect fluid has a local rest frame with energy density \(\epsilon\), isotropic pressure \(p\), and no heat flux or viscous stress. Its continuum description is useful when a small fluid element contains many particles yet is small compared with macroscopic gradients.
statement: A perfect fluid has isotropic rest-frame pressure and no heat flux or viscous shear stress.

title: Build the covariant tensor
body:
With signature \(+---\) and \(g(u,u)=c^2\), the model is \[T^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{perfect fluid}}{=} rac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}u^\mu u^
u-pg^{\mu
u}.\] In the local fluid rest frame, \(u^{\hat\mu}=(c,0,0,0)\), so \(T^{\hat\mu\hat
u}=\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon,p,p,p)\). The minus metric term gives positive spatial pressures in this signature.
statement:
With \(+---\), a perfect fluid has \(T^{\mu
u}=(\epsilon+p)u^\mu u^
u/c^2-pg^{\mu
u}\).

title: Dust and radiation
body: Dust neglects pressure and gives \(T^{\mu\nu}=\epsilon u^\mu u^\nu/c^2\), with \(\epsilon\simeq\rho c^2\) when rest mass dominates. Isotropic radiation instead has \(p=\epsilon/3\). Both fit the same tensor form, but their matter response differs through their \cref{equation of state}{gr.equation_of_state}.
statement: Dust and isotropic radiation share the perfect-fluid tensor form but have different pressures.

title: Project conservation along the flow
body:
For a perfect fluid, define the derivative along the flow by \(D\coloneqq u^\mu
abla_\mu\) and its expansion by \(	heta\coloneqq
abla_\mu u^\mu\). Assume the total fluid stress-energy obeys \(
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0\).

Contract that equation with \(u_
u\). Expanding the perfect-fluid tensor gives
\[ egin{aligned}0&=D(\epsilon+p)+(\epsilon+p)	heta-Dp\ &=D\epsilon+(\epsilon+p)	heta.\end{aligned}\]
The terms containing \(u_
u Du^
u\) vanish because the velocity norm is fixed and the connection is metric-compatible. The two derivatives of pressure cancel, leaving the energy balance.

If a comoving element has volume \(V\) with \(DV=	heta V\), this says \(D(\epsilon V)=-p\,DV\): energy decreases as the element does pressure work while expanding. This interpretation connects the tensor equation to thermodynamics.

\explanation{pressure-acceleration}{Why need a perfect fluid not follow geodesics?}{Project conservation perpendicular to \(u\). With \(h^{\alpha
u}=g^{\alpha
u}-u^\alpha u^
u/c^2\), it gives
\[ rac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}a^\alpha=h^{\alpha
u}
abla_
u p.\]
In the local rest frame the spatial projector is negative, so the fluid accelerates down a pressure gradient. Only when the relevant pressure force vanishes, as for freely moving dust, does this equation reduce to geodesic motion.}
statement: The velocity projection of fluid conservation balances changing energy density against expansion and pressure work.

title: Perfect does not mean pressureless or geodesic
body: The absence of viscosity is not the absence of pressure. Pressure gradients can accelerate the fluid, so its elements need not follow geodesics. Freely moving dust does follow geodesics wherever its density is nonzero, until effects such as stream crossing invalidate a single-fluid velocity description.
statement: A perfect fluid may have pressure gradients and accelerated motion; perfect does not mean dust.

title: State the matter assumptions of a theorem
body: Energy conditions impose inequalities on stress-energy. They make assumptions such as nonnegative observer energy or causal energy flow precise. They are additional hypotheses, not identities or consequences of Einstein's equations.
statement: Energy conditions are additional inequalities imposed on matter, not consequences of Einstein’s equations.

title: Null and weak conditions
body:
The null energy condition (NEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}k^\mu k^
u\geq0\) for every null \(k\). The weak energy condition (WEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) for every timelike \(v\). Normalising \(v\) turns the latter into nonnegative measured energy density. By continuity WEC implies NEC.
statement: NEC tests nonnegative null contractions; WEC tests nonnegative energy for every timelike observer.

title: Dominant and strong conditions
body:
With \(+---\), the dominant energy condition (DEC) requires \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^\mu{}_{
u}v^
u\) to be future-directed causal or zero for every future timelike \(v\). The strong energy condition (SEC) requires \((T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u})v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) in four dimensions. Through the field equations with zero cosmological constant, SEC gives the Ricci convergence condition used in focusing arguments. With \(\Lambda
e0\), include its effective source before drawing that conclusion.
statement: DEC requires causal future energy flow; SEC requires a nonnegative trace-adjusted timelike contraction.

title: Perfect-fluid tests
body:
For a perfect fluid the conditions reduce to: NEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\); WEC, also \(\epsilon\geq0\); DEC, \(\epsilon\geq|p|\); SEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\) and \(\epsilon+3p\geq0\). These follow by testing rest-frame and highly boosted observers. Positive vacuum energy has \(p=-\epsilon\), so it satisfies NEC, WEC and DEC but violates SEC.

\explanation{boosted-fluid-energy}{Why must the weak condition test boosted observers too?}{In the fluid rest frame, a unit observer moving at speed \(v\) measures \(\gamma^2(\epsilon+p)-p\), with \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\). At rest this is \(\epsilon\), requiring \(\epsilon\geq0\). For arbitrarily large boosts the coefficient \(\epsilon+p\) must also be nonnegative. Together these give the perfect-fluid WEC, not merely positivity in one frame.}
statement: For a perfect fluid, the conditions reduce to inequalities involving \(\epsilon\), \(\epsilon+p\) and \(\epsilon+3p\).

title: Names do not form a strength ranking
body: The strong condition is not stronger than the weak condition in the logical sense. Classical models can violate some conditions, and quantum expectation values can violate pointwise conditions too. A theorem using one remains conditional on that precise assumption; failure of the assumption alone neither proves nor disproves the theorem's conclusion.
statement: The names weak, dominant and strong do not define a simple hierarchy of increasingly restrictive conditions.

title: Balance includes geometric comparison
body: Local energy-momentum balance must compare tensor quantities at neighbouring events. In curved spacetime the connection supplies that comparison. For the total matter source with its equations of motion satisfied, the conservation statement is \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\).
statement: Local energy–momentum balance compares neighbouring stress-energy using the spacetime connection.

title: Expand the divergence
body:
The total matter and nongravitational-field source obeys
\[
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0\]
when its equations of motion are satisfied. “On shell” means those matter equations hold. Expanding the tensor derivative gives
\[ egin{aligned}
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}&=\partial_\mu T^{\mu
u}\ &\quad+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda
u}\ &\quad+\Gamma^
u{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}.\end{aligned}\]
There are two corrections because stress-energy has two upper indices. The \cref{covariant derivative}{gr.covariant_derivative.definition} compares the source in neighbouring tangent spaces; ordinary component divergence alone would not express coordinate-independent balance. Interacting subsystems may exchange energy and need not satisfy zero divergence separately.
statement: For the complete on-shell matter source, local balance is \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\).

title: Consistency of the coupled equations
body:
For a coupled solution, write Einstein's equation as \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}\), with constant \(\Lambda\). Take its covariant divergence:
\[ egin{aligned}\kappa
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}&=
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\ &\quad-\Lambda
abla^\mu g_{\mu
u}\ &=0.\end{aligned}\]
The first term vanishes by the contracted Bianchi identity, the second by metric compatibility. This is a consistency check on the coupled equations, not a prescription for what matter is present.

There is also an independent matter-action argument: coordinate invariance of the complete matter action, with the matter equations imposed, implies the same balance law. So one need not assume Einstein's equations before formulating matter conservation. A subsystem that exchanges energy with another field instead has a corresponding nonzero exchange term.
statement: Bianchi and metric compatibility make Einstein’s field equation consistent only with a conserved total source.

title: A symmetry can supply a conserved charge
body:
If a vector field \(\xi\) generates an isometry, it obeys the Killing equation \(
abla_\mu\xi_
u+
abla_
u\xi_\mu=0\). Symmetry of stress-energy then makes \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^{\mu
u}\xi_
u\) divergence-free. Integrating this vector current gives a conserved charge when boundary flux vanishes. A timelike symmetry supplies an energy interpretation.

\explanation{killing-current}{Check the symmetry cancellation}{Differentiate \(J^\mu=T^{\mu
u}\xi_
u\). Conservation removes \((
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u})\xi_
u\). Symmetry of \(T\) then writes the remainder as \(	frac12T^{\mu
u}(
abla_\mu\xi_
u+
abla_
u\xi_\mu)\), which vanishes by the Killing equation. A conserved integrated charge still requires suitable slices and control of boundary flux.}
statement: A Killing symmetry converts symmetric conserved stress-energy into a divergence-free vector current.

title: Local balance is not universal global energy
body: A generic spacetime has no time-translation symmetry. One cannot simply add coordinate energy components at different events and infer a conserved total from the tensor divergence. Boundary or asymptotic constructions can provide gravitational energy in appropriate settings, but require additional structure.
statement: Without time-translation symmetry or suitable boundary structure, local balance does not imply a universal total energy.

title: Supply material physics
body: Einstein's equations couple geometry to matter but do not specify how a material's pressure depends on its thermodynamic state. An equation of state supplies this constitutive information. Together with conservation and a fluid model, it closes the evolution problem.
statement: An equation of state adds material information needed to close a fluid’s equations.

title: A simple barotropic model
body: A barotropic fluid assumes \(p=p(\epsilon)\), where \(\epsilon\) is rest-frame energy density. A useful idealisation is the model law \[p=w\epsilon,\qquad w\coloneqq p/\epsilon\quad(\epsilon\ne0).\] The first equation assumes constant \(w\) when used as a linear equation of state; the ratio definition alone does not assert that constancy. Pressure and energy density have the same units.
statement: A barotropic model assumes \(p=p(\epsilon)\); constant \(w\) gives the special law \(p=w\epsilon\).

title: Three distinct responses
body: Pressureless dust uses \(w=0\); isotropic radiation uses \(w=1/3\); an effective cosmological source uses \(w=-1\). The last is not an ordinary gas with a preferred fluid rest frame. These examples are material assumptions or idealisations, rather than alternatives to the gravitational field equation.
statement: Dust, isotropic radiation and effective vacuum energy have \(w=0\), \(1/3\) and \(-1\), respectively.

title: Count the missing relation
body:
On a given metric, a perfect fluid has energy density, pressure and three independent velocity components. Its four conservation equations leave one constitutive relation to supply. More general materials need additional variables such as particle density, entropy or composition, with their own equations; a single barotropic relation is then insufficient.

\explanation{five-variables}{Why are there only three velocity variables?}{Four-velocity has four components, but \(g(u,u)=c^2\) imposes one relation. Choosing future direction leaves three independent velocity components. Adding \(\epsilon\) and \(p\) gives five variables. The four components of conservation therefore do not by themselves tell the fluid how pressure changes with energy density.}
statement: Four conservation equations leave one relation missing among a perfect fluid’s five independent local variables.

title: Sound speed is a derivative
body: For adiabatic perturbations of a suitable ordinary fluid, \(c_s^2=c^2(\partial p/\partial\epsilon)_s\), where entropy per particle is held fixed. Thus a constant barotropic law gives \(c_s^2=wc^2\). Stability and causal propagation constrain the derivative, not just the ratio \(p/\epsilon\). Do not interpret the vacuum relation \(w=-1\) as the sound speed of an ordinary fluid.
statement: Adiabatic sound speed depends on the pressure derivative, rather than merely on \(p/\epsilon\).

title: Couple geometry and matter
body:
Given a distribution of matter, we want to determine clocks, rulers, light cones and free-fall paths. These are all controlled by the metric. But the matter's motion also depends on that metric, so geometry and matter must be solved together.

The \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} supplies a curvature combination with the right local divergence identity. The \cref{stress-energy tensor}{gr.stress_energy_tensor} supplies the source. A constant metric term permits a cosmological constant.

Choosing this relation is physical input. The action formulation organises it, and the Newtonian limit calibrates its coupling; neither general covariance nor the equivalence principle alone uniquely derives Einstein's theory.
statement: Einstein’s equations couple a dynamical metric to the energy, momentum and stress of matter.

title: The atlas field equation
body:
With signature \(+---\), the glossary's Riemann definition and explicit \(c\), define \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G/c^4\). The field equation is \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The minus sign before \(\Lambda\) belongs to this complete convention; positive \(\Lambda\) represents positive effective vacuum energy. Sources using the opposite signature often write a plus sign. Comparing signs requires comparing curvature definitions too.
statement:
The atlas uses \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=(8\pi G/c^4)T_{\mu
u}\), with its stated curvature convention.

title: Why this combination works
body:
The \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and constant metric term have zero covariant divergence. Their source must therefore obey \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation}. The coupling is fixed by recovering Newton's Poisson equation for weak, slowly varying fields and nonrelativistic matter. Pressure and radiation remain sources beyond that limit.

\explanation{why-pressure}{Why does pressure appear when Newtonian gravity mainly uses mass density?}{Pressure represents momentum transfer, so it belongs to the same relativistic tensor as energy density. Newtonian matter usually has pressure small compared with \(\rho c^2\), hiding its contribution at leading order. In relativistic matter that approximation fails; the full tensor is needed rather than a mass-density-only source.}
statement: The curvature divergence identity matches source conservation, while the Newtonian limit fixes the coupling.

title: Equations need data and a matter model
body: There are ten symmetric component equations in four dimensions, linked by four differential identities and coordinate freedom. Their initial-value formulation contains constraints as well as evolution equations. Solving requires appropriate initial or boundary data, a coordinate choice and matter dynamics; conservation alone does not select a unique spacetime.
statement: A solution needs matter dynamics, coordinate choices and initial or boundary data in addition to the field equation.

title: Vacuum is not the absence of gravitational physics
body: Where \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), curvature can still encode tides and gravitational waves. Nonlinear metric terms describe gravitational self-interaction without inserting a universal local gravitational stress-energy tensor on the right. The \cref{trace-reversed form}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} is often easier for calculations but describes the same theory.
statement: Vacuum can contain tidal curvature and gravitational waves despite a vanishing local matter source.

title: A uniform geometric term
body: The cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) permits curvature even without ordinary matter. It has dimensions of inverse length squared and multiplies the metric, introducing no preferred observer direction at an event.
statement: A constant metric-proportional term permits spacetime curvature without ordinary matter.

title: Move it to an effective source
body:
The cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) is a spacetime-independent parameter with dimensions of inverse length squared. In the atlas equation it appears as
\[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\]
Moving it to the right is equivalent to adding an effective source
\[T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu
u}\coloneqq rac{\Lambda}{\kappa}g_{\mu
u}.\]
This is an algebraic reassignment of the same term, not a second source to be counted again. Its metric-proportional form introduces no preferred timelike direction at an event. If vacuum energy is already included in \(T\), do not also include it in \(\Lambda\).
statement: The cosmological constant multiplies the metric and can equivalently be represented as \(T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu\nu}=\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}/\kappa\).

title: Read its density and pressure
body:
For an observer with \(g(u,u)=c^2\), contracting \(T^{(\Lambda)}=(\Lambda/\kappa)g\) gives
\[\epsilon_\Lambda=\frac{T^{(\Lambda)}(u,u)}{c^2}=\frac{\Lambda}{\kappa}.\]
Using \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\), this is \(\epsilon_\Lambda=\Lambda c^4/(8\pi G)\). Every such observer obtains the same value because the contraction depends only on the fixed velocity norm.

Compare with the perfect-fluid form. Setting \(p_\Lambda=-\epsilon_\Lambda\) removes the \(u^\mu u^\nu\) term and leaves \(T^{\mu\nu}=\epsilon_\Lambda g^{\mu\nu}\). Thus the effective source has negative pressure and no distinguished fluid rest frame. It is not an ordinary gas with a negative sound-speed squared.
statement: Positive \(\Lambda\) represents positive effective vacuum energy with pressure \(p_\Lambda=-\epsilon_\Lambda\).

title: Curved empty spacetime
body: In four-dimensional ordinary vacuum, tracing the field equation gives \(R=-4\Lambda\) and hence \(R_{\mu\nu}=-\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}\) in our convention. Positive \(\Lambda\) permits de Sitter geometry and contributes an outward acceleration \(\Lambda c^2r/3\) in the weak static spherical limit. The sign of the Ricci scalar alone must not be used to infer attraction.
statement: Ordinary vacuum with nonzero \(\Lambda\) is not Ricci-flat; positive \(\Lambda\) gives de Sitter-type repulsion.

title: The equation does not explain the value
body: A metric-proportional source can model vacuum energy, but classical GR does not determine its microscopic origin or numerical value. Cosmological observations and quantum vacuum-energy calculations are separate subjects. A spacetime-varying replacement needs extra dynamics or energy exchange to remain compatible with the Bianchi identity.
statement: Classical GR permits a cosmological constant but does not determine its microscopic origin or value.

title: Measure matter's response to geometry
body: Changing the metric changes distances, volume and the contractions in a matter action. The coefficient of that variation defines the Hilbert stress-energy tensor. This construction makes its role as the gravitational source explicit.
statement: Hilbert stress-energy measures the first-order response of the matter action to a change in the metric.

title: Vary the inverse metric
body:
Use natural units \(c=1\) and signature \(+---\). Hold the matter fields fixed while varying the inverse metric. The Hilbert tensor is defined by
\[T_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta S_m}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}.\]
Equivalently,
\[\delta S_m=\tfrac12\int dV_4\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}.\]
The functional derivative includes any integrations by parts needed to isolate the metric variation. This positive source sign pairs with the atlas's negative gravitational action. Symmetry follows because the varied metric is symmetric; conservation additionally uses matter dynamics.
statement: With \(c=1\) and fixed matter fields, our source convention is \(\delta S_m=\tfrac12\int dV_4\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}\).

title: A minimally coupled scalar example
body:
Take \(S_m=\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal L_m\), where \(\mathcal L_m\coloneqq	frac12g^{\alpha eta}\partial_\alpha\phi\partial_ eta\phi-V(\phi)\). Varying both the contraction and the determinant gives \[T_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_
u\phi-g_{\mu
u}\mathcal L_m.\] The first contribution comes from \(g^{\alpha eta}\); the second from \(\sqrt{-g}\). Omitting the volume variation gives the wrong source.

\explanation{scalar-first-variation}{Separate the two contributions}{With the matter field held fixed, \(\delta\mathcal L_m=	frac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial_
u\phi\,\delta g^{\mu
u}\). The determinant contributes \(-	frac12\mathcal L_m g_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}\). Multiplying each by \(\sqrt{-g}\), adding them and comparing with the defining variation gives the tensor. Neither contribution can be discarded.}
statement:
A minimally coupled scalar gives \(T_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu\phi\partial_
u\phi-g_{\mu
u}\mathcal L_m\).

title: Check physical energy
body:
Use the minimally coupled scalar Lagrangian \(\mathcal L_m=\tfrac12g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_\alpha\phi\partial_\beta\phi-V\), in natural units. In a local orthonormal frame define \(\dot\phi=\partial_{\hat0}\phi\) and \(s^2=\sum_i(\partial_{\hat i}\phi)^2\). Then
\[\begin{aligned}\mathcal L_m&=\tfrac12\dot\phi^2-\tfrac12s^2-V,\\ T_{\hat0\hat0}&=\dot\phi^2-\mathcal L_m\\ &=\tfrac12\dot\phi^2+\tfrac12s^2+V.\end{aligned}\]
The kinetic and spatial-gradient terms are nonnegative, so \(V\geq0\) ensures a nonnegative measured density. This is a useful sign check on the chosen action and metric-variation convention, rather than a proof of every energy condition.
statement: The scalar-field tensor has nonnegative local energy density when its potential is nonnegative.

title: Changing the varied variable changes a sign
body:
Because \(\delta g^{\mu
u}=-g^{\mu\alpha}g^{
u eta}\delta g_{\alpha eta}\), varying the covariant metric instead gives \(\delta S_m=-	frac12\int\sqrt{-g}\,T^{\mu
u}\delta g_{\mu
u}\,d^4x\). Symmetry of the metric variation gives a symmetric tensor. Its covariant conservation additionally uses the matter equations, not merely this definition.
statement: Changing from inverse-metric to covariant-metric variation reverses the sign of the source coefficient.

title: Solve algebraically for Ricci
body: Trace reversal rewrites Einstein's equations as a direct relation between Ricci curvature and a trace-adjusted source. It changes the algebraic packaging, not the theory, and is particularly useful in the Newtonian and vacuum limits.
statement: Trace reversal rewrites the same field equation as a direct equation for the Ricci tensor.

title: Take the four-dimensional trace
body:
Define \(T=g^{\mu
u}T_{\mu
u}\). In four dimensions, the trace-reversed form of the atlas field equation is
\[ egin{aligned}R_{\mu
u}&=\kappa igl(T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u} igr)\ &\quad-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
It is algebraically equivalent to Einstein's original equation, not a different source model. To see where the trace term comes from, contract the original equation with \(g^{\mu
u}\). Since the trace of the identity is four, the result is \(-R-4\Lambda=\kappa T\), or \(R=-\kappa T-4\Lambda\).
statement:
In four dimensions, \(R_{\mu
u}=\kappa(T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u})-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\).

title: Substitute the trace back
body:
Start with \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}\), where \(G_{\mu
u}=R_{\mu
u}-Rg_{\mu
u}/2\). Its four-dimensional trace gives \(R=-\kappa T-4\Lambda\).

Now isolate the Ricci tensor in the original equation and insert that scalar result:
\[ egin{aligned}R_{\mu
u}&=\kappa T_{\mu
u}+	frac12Rg_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\ &=\kappa T_{\mu
u}-	frac\kappa2Tg_{\mu
u}\ &\quad-2\Lambda g_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\ &=\kappa igl(T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u} igr)\ &\quad-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
Thus the field equation and the definition of Ricci combine through a trace and a substitution. The adjusted source is algebraically useful, but it is the original \(T\) that has the direct energy–momentum interpretation.
statement: Taking the field equation’s trace and substituting it back isolates Ricci without changing the theory.

title: Pressure remains in the source
body: For a perfect fluid in its orthonormal rest frame, \(T=\epsilon-3p\). Therefore \[R_{\hat0\hat0}\overset{\text{perfect fluid}}{=}\frac{\kappa}{2}(\epsilon+3p)-\Lambda.\] This helps explain why relativistic pressure gravitates. It is a local curvature relation, not by itself an equation for a star's total mass.
statement: For a perfect fluid, \(R_{\hat0\hat0}=\kappa(\epsilon+3p)/2-\Lambda\) in its rest frame.

title: The coefficient depends on dimension
body: In \(n>2\) dimensions the source trace coefficient is \(1/(n-2)\), and the cosmological term here is \(-2\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}/(n-2)\). The familiar one half is specific to four dimensions. In two dimensions this inversion fails because the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.
statement: The coefficient one-half is specific to four dimensions; trace reversal fails in two dimensions.

title: Remove matter locally, not curvature
body: An ordinary vacuum region has \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\). It can lie outside a star or black hole even though matter elsewhere helped determine its geometry. Vacuum is a local source condition, not a statement that nothing gravitational happens there.
statement: Vacuum removes the local matter source, while permitting tidal curvature determined by the geometry and data.

title: Zero cosmological constant
body: In four dimensions with \(\Lambda=0\), the field equation gives \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\). Taking the trace yields \(R=0\), so \[R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0.\] This is Ricci-flatness. It constrains a contraction of Riemann, leaving possible Weyl curvature and tidal effects.
statement: With zero cosmological constant, four-dimensional vacuum Einstein equations are equivalent to \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\).

title: Schwarzschild is curved vacuum
body: Outside a spherical body the Schwarzschild solution has zero Ricci tensor but \(K=48(GM/c^2)^2/r^6\). Thus a freely falling cloud can deform despite the absence of local matter. \cref{Gravitational waves}{gr.gravitational_waves} also illustrate vacuum curvature carrying physical tidal information.
statement: Schwarzschild and gravitational waves show that vacuum need not be flat.

title: Retaining the cosmological term
body:
With ordinary matter absent but \(\Lambda
e0\), the atlas trace-reversed equation instead gives \[R_{\mu
u}\overset{T_{\mu
u}=0}{=}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\] This is not Ricci-flat. State whether vacuum includes an explicit cosmological term or whether that term has been absorbed into an effective stress-energy source.
statement: With ordinary matter absent but nonzero \(\Lambda\), vacuum instead obeys \(R_{\mu\nu}=-\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}\).

title: Vacuum equations do not select Schwarzschild alone
body: A solution still needs symmetry assumptions and suitable data. Schwarzschild describes spherical vacuum with zero cosmological constant; rotating or time-dependent vacuum geometries need not share its form. Boundary conditions retain information about sources outside the region in which the vacuum equation is being solved.
statement: Vacuum equations require symmetry and suitable data before selecting a particular spacetime such as Schwarzschild.

title: Approximate a region by a flat background
body:
Local flatness lets us make a smooth metric Minkowskian at one event. Weak-field theory asks for more: a whole region should admit suitable coordinates in which the metric differs only slightly from a flat background.

Write \(g=\eta+h\). Keeping first order in the small perturbation \(h\) makes many calculations manageable while retaining nonzero curvature. This is useful both for the nearly static field far from a star and for small-amplitude waves.

Weak field alone does not mean slow motion. Light remains relativistic, and a small wave can vary rapidly. To obtain Newtonian motion we must add further assumptions about speeds, source stresses and time variation.

\explanation{amplitude-curvature}{Does a small perturbation guarantee tiny curvature?}{Curvature involves derivatives, not only amplitude. A small perturbation varying over a short wavelength can have appreciable second derivatives. The validity of a linear approximation requires the neglected products to remain small relative to the retained terms in the calculation being made.}
statement: Weak-field theory assumes a metric close to Minkowski form over a useful region, not merely at one event.

title: Choose a background split
body:
Define the perturbation by \(h_{\mu
u}\coloneqq g_{\mu
u}-\eta_{\mu
u}\), with \(|h_{\mu
u}|\ll1\) in the chosen background chart. To first order, \[g^{\mu
u}\simeq\eta^{\mu
u}-h^{\mu
u},\qquad h^{\mu
u}\coloneqq\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}h_{\alpha eta}.\] Multiplying this inverse by \(g_{\mu
u}\) cancels the linear correction; products of perturbations are discarded.
statement:
A chosen background split \(g_{\mu
u}=\eta_{\mu
u}+h_{\mu
u}\) is linearised by discarding products of perturbations.

title: Connection and curvature at first order
body:
Insert \(g_{\mu
u}=\eta_{\mu
u}+h_{\mu
u}\) into the Levi-Civita formula. The background metric is constant, and replacing the inverse metric by \(\eta^{ho\sigma}\) incurs only a second-order correction because it multiplies a derivative of \(h\).

Define
\[ egin{aligned}C_{\sigma\mu
u}&=\partial_\mu h_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u h_{\sigma\mu}\ &\quad-\partial_\sigma h_{\mu
u}.\end{aligned}\]
Then \(\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\simeq	frac12\eta^{ho\sigma}C_{\sigma\mu
u}\). In Riemann's formula, differentiating this gives terms with two derivatives of \(h\), while the products \(\Gamma\Gamma\) are second order and are omitted.

Thus the metric split supplies both the connection correction and its tidal curvature. Linearisation simplifies the geometry; it does not set the geometry flat.
statement: At first order, the connection contains first derivatives of \(h\) and curvature contains second derivatives.

title: A static Newtonian source
body:
For slowly moving matter with negligible pressure and anisotropic stress, neglect \(\Lambda\) and choose isotropic spatial coordinates. Write \(d\ell^2=\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j\). A suitable weak-field metric is
\[\begin{aligned}ds^2&\simeq(1+2\Phi/c^2)c^2dt^2\\ &\quad-(1-2\Phi/c^2)d\ell^2.\end{aligned}\]
The potential \(\Phi\) is negative near an isolated positive mass when it vanishes at infinity. The temporal correction governs leading stationary clock-rate differences. The spatial correction also affects null paths; omitting it loses half the leading light deflection in this chart.

These components describe a specific weak-field solution and coordinate choice, not every possible small perturbation.
statement: A weak static source perturbs both the temporal and spatial parts of the metric.

title: Gauge and approximation are different choices
body: A small coordinate change changes the components of \(h\), so their smallness is assessed in an appropriate chart, not every possible chart. Linearisation discards nonlinear terms after that choice. The \cref{Newtonian limit}{gr.newtonian_limit} adds slow motion and approximate stationarity; the \cref{post-Newtonian scheme}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} keeps selected nonlinear terms consistently.
statement: Gauge choice changes perturbation components; linearisation separately decides which orders to retain.

title: Recover both motion and the source law
body: The Newtonian limit requires a weak, approximately stationary field, slow test bodies and nonrelativistic sources whose pressure is small compared with rest energy. Set \(\Lambda=0\) for the ordinary Poisson law. Recovering acceleration alone is only half the check.
statement: Recovering Newtonian gravity requires both the inverse-square motion law and the Poisson source equation.

title: The metric gives the force law
body:
With \(x^0=ct\) and \(g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi/c^2\), the static connection gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq\partial_i\Phi/c^2\). The dominant part of the spatial geodesic equation is therefore \[\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}\simeq-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq-\partial_i\Phi.\] Slow motion suppresses terms involving spatial velocities; weak fields let proper time and coordinate time agree to the required order.

\explanation{connection-sign}{Check the attractive sign}{The static formula gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq-\tfrac12\eta^{ij}\partial_j h_{00}\). Since \(\eta^{ij}=-\delta^{ij}\) and \(h_{00}=2\Phi/c^2\), this is \(+\partial_i\Phi/c^2\). The minus sign in the geodesic equation then yields acceleration down the potential gradient.}
statement: The leading spatial geodesic equation gives \(d^2x^i/dt^2\simeq-\partial_i\Phi\).

title: The field equation gives Poisson's law
body:
With \(x^0=ct\), the weak static metric gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq\partial_i\Phi/c^2\). In Ricci, the surviving leading term is its spatial divergence:
\[R_{00}\simeq\partial_i\Gamma^i{}_{00}=\frac{\nabla^2\Phi}{c^2}.\]
For low-pressure, slowly moving matter, \(T_{00}\simeq\rho c^2\) and \(T\simeq\rho c^2\), where \(\rho\) is mass density. The \cref{trace-reversed field equation}{gr.trace_reversed_equations.definition} therefore becomes
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{\nabla^2\Phi}{c^2}&\simeq\kappa(\rho c^2-\tfrac12\rho c^2)\\ &=\tfrac\kappa2\rho c^2.\end{aligned}\]
Matching Newton's source law fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\), giving \(\nabla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi G\rho\). Thus the field equation supplies the source law, while the geodesic equation separately supplies the test-body motion law.
statement: The weak static time-time Ricci equation becomes Poisson’s law and fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\).

title: An isolated spherical source
body: Outside the source, spherical symmetry and zero potential at infinity give \(\Phi=-GM/r\) in Newtonian theory. Its gradient produces inward acceleration \(-GM\mathbf x/r^3\). Inserting this potential into \(g_{00}\) also predicts the leading slowing of stationary clocks nearer the mass.
statement: An isolated spherical source has \(\Phi=-GM/r\), giving inward inverse-square acceleration and slower nearby clocks.

title: Keep the limits distinct
body: Small potential does not make light slow or radiation pressure negligible. The Newtonian motion approximation fails for light, even when linearised gravity remains valid. If \(\Lambda\) is retained, the same convention gives \(\nabla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi G\rho-\Lambda c^2\); the ordinary inverse-square result assumes that extra term is negligible.
statement: Weak fields can still involve relativistic light or pressure, so they need not admit Newtonian dynamics.

title: Compare emission and reception clocks
body:
Imagine one clock emitting successive light pulses and another counting their arrivals. Each clock measures its own proper time. In a static field the two proper-time rates can differ, so the same train of pulses can have different emission and reception frequencies.

The key inputs are the \cref{proper-time measuring rule}{gr.proper_time.definition} and the static metric's time-translation symmetry. The weak metric then gives a useful leading formula in terms of the Newtonian potential.

Neither observer measures light locally travelling at anything other than \(c\). The frequency comparison concerns how many wave crests arrive per unit local clock time, not a local slowing of light.
statement: Stationary clocks at different gravitational potentials assign different frequencies to exchanged light.

title: Stationary proper-time rates
body:
Gravitational redshift is a frequency difference associated with gravitational clock-rate differences, after the observers and signal protocol are specified. For stationary emission at \(A\) and reception at \(B\) in a static chart with \(x^0=ct\),
\[\frac{\nu_B}{\nu_A}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{00}(A)}{g_{00}(B)}}.\]
Each clock has \(d\tau=\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt\). The common coordinate time is tied to the static symmetry; it is not the reading of every local clock. The formula assumes \(g_{00}>0\) along the stationary observers and no relative coordinate motion.
statement: For stationary observers in a static metric, \(\nu_B/\nu_A=\sqrt{g_{00}(A)/g_{00}(B)}\).

title: Use successive wave crests
body:
Time-translation symmetry makes successive crests take the same coordinate travel time, so their emission and reception coordinate intervals agree. Dividing by the local proper-time rates gives \[\frac{\nu_B}{\nu_A}\overset{\text{static exchange}}{=}\sqrt{\frac{g_{00}(A)}{g_{00}(B)}}.\] Here \(A\) emits and \(B\) receives. This static formula is exact, not restricted to a weak field.

\explanation{counting-crests}{Make the clock comparison explicit}{Let \(\Delta t\) separate emissions of two crests. Static symmetry makes the second crest's travel time equal to the first's, so arrivals also differ by \(\Delta t\). The clocks instead record \(\Delta\tau_A=\sqrt{g_{00}(A)}\Delta t\) and \(\Delta\tau_B=\sqrt{g_{00}(B)}\Delta t\). Frequency is inverse period; dividing those periods gives the stated ratio.}
statement: Equal coordinate intervals between successive wave crests become unequal proper-time intervals at the endpoints.

title: A small height difference
statement: A receiver a small height \(h\) above the emitter measures a fractional redshift \(-g_{\mathrm{acc}}h/c^2\).

title: Do not apply the static formula to arbitrary observers
body: Motion adds Doppler effects, and a time-dependent geometry need not preserve the coordinate interval argument. Even a static chart ceases to describe physical stationary observers where its time direction becomes null or spacelike, as at and inside a Schwarzschild horizon. The conserved photon quantity associated with time symmetry is distinct from the energy measured by each local observer.
statement: Observer motion, time-dependent geometry and failure of a static observer change the frequency comparison.

title: Follow null geodesics
body: In geometric optics, freely propagating light follows null geodesics of the metric. A weak isolated mass changes their direction relative to distant incoming and outgoing reference lines. No photon rest mass or material refractive medium is required.
statement: A curved metric changes the direction of null geodesics relative to distant incoming and outgoing rays.

title: The weak scattering setup
body:
For a static spherical mass \(M\), light deflection is the angle between distant incoming and outgoing ray directions. With source and observer far from the mass, the leading weak-field result is
\[\alpha\simeq\frac{4GM}{bc^2}.\]
The impact parameter \(b\) is the offset of the incoming asymptotic line. It equals the closest approach radius only at leading order. Assume \(GM/(bc^2)\ll1\), geometric optics, and negligible rotation, other masses and cosmological curvature.

This is a null-geodesic effect. A photon rest mass or a material refractive medium is not part of the explanation.
statement: Weak spherical light deflection is the small asymptotic change in ray direction, \(\alpha\simeq4GM/(bc^2)\).

title: The full weak metric doubles the gradient term
body:
From the isotropic weak-field metric and \(ds^2=0\), \(c\,dt\simeq(1-2\Phi/c^2)d\ell\). Thus the coordinate optical path has an effective index \(n\simeq1-2\Phi/c^2\). This is a computational description of geometry, not a local change in light speed. The transverse ray change is \(\Delta\mathbf e_\perp\simeq-2c^{-2}\int\nabla_\perp\Phi\,dz\) along the unperturbed line.

\explanation{optical-factor}{Why is the factor two present?}{Using \(ds^2=0\) in the isotropic weak metric gives
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{c\,dt}{d\ell}&=\sqrt{\frac{1-2\Phi/c^2}{1+2\Phi/c^2}}\\ &\simeq1-2\Phi/c^2.\end{aligned}\]
One factor comes from the spatial measuring rule and one from the temporal rule. This optical index is a coordinate calculation device for the same null paths; a local observer still measures light speed \(c\).}
statement: Both weak-metric perturbations contribute to an effective optical index \(n\simeq1-2\Phi/c^2\).

title: Integrate a point-mass potential
body:
Take the unperturbed ray along \(z\), at transverse offset \(b\). With \(\Phi=-GM/\sqrt{b^2+z^2}\), the optical-path equation gives a bending magnitude
\[\alpha\simeq\frac{2GMb}{c^2}I,\]
where
\[I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{2}{b^2}.\]
So \(\alpha\simeq4GM/(bc^2)\), directed towards the mass. Evaluating along the undeflected line is consistent at first order: changing that line would correct an already first-order integrand at higher order.

\explanation{bending-integral}{Evaluate the integral}{An antiderivative is \(z/[b^2\sqrt{b^2+z^2}]\). At positive infinity it tends to \(1/b^2\), and at negative infinity to \(-1/b^2\). Their difference is \(2/b^2\).}
statement: Integrating the transverse point-mass potential gradient gives the leading deflection \(4GM/(bc^2)\).

title: Stay outside the strong-deflection regime
body: The result is first order in \(GM/(bc^2)\). Close to the photon sphere, multiple turns and capture require the full null-geodesic equations. A \cref{Newtonian slow-body calculation}{gr.newtonian_limit} cannot be applied to light to obtain the missing spatial contribution.
statement: Strong bending and capture require full null-geodesic dynamics, not the leading weak-deflection formula.

title: Radial and angular periods separate
body: In Newtonian inverse-square gravity, a bound test orbit is a closed ellipse. Schwarzschild geodesics add a small mismatch between radial oscillation and angular revolution, so the closest-approach direction advances. For other central bodies the same effect is called periapsis advance.
statement: Relativistic orbital motion separates the radial and angular periods, advancing the closest-approach direction.

title: The orbit equation exposes the correction
body: Use \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), a test body, spherical nonrotating geometry and \(\Lambda=0\). Let \(q\coloneqq1/r\) and \(\ell\coloneqq r^2d\phi/d\tau\) be specific angular momentum. The timelike Schwarzschild geodesic equation reduces to \[\frac{d^2q}{d\phi^2}+q\overset{\text{Schwarzschild geodesic}}{=}\frac{GM}{\ell^2}+3mq^2.\] The last term is absent from the Kepler problem. The inverse radius is called \(q\) here to avoid confusing it with four-velocity \(u^\mu\).
statement: The spherical timelike geodesic orbit equation contains an extra \(3mq^2\) term beyond Kepler motion.

title: Find the frequency shift
body:
Take the spherical timelike geodesic equation as input:
\[q''+q=\frac1{p_{\mathrm{orb}}}+3mq^2,\]
where \(q=1/r\), primes mean \(d/d\phi\), \(m=GM/c^2\), and \(p_{\mathrm{orb}}=\ell^2/(GM)\) at leading order. Begin with the Kepler ellipse \(q_0=(1+e\cos\phi)/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\).

Its square contributes a resonant term \(6me\cos\phi/p_{\mathrm{orb}}^2\). Now try a slightly shifted frequency,
\[q\simeq\frac{1+e\cos[(1-\delta)\phi]}{p_{\mathrm{orb}}}.\]
To first order in \(\delta\), the cosine part of \(q''+q\) has coefficient \(2\delta e/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\). Matching the resonant coefficients gives \(\delta=3m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\).

The remaining constant and double-frequency corrections alter the detailed orbit shape but do not change this leading frequency shift. The result assumes \(m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\ll1\); it is not an exact strong-field orbit solution.

\explanation{resonant-term}{Why focus on the matching cosine?}{A forcing term at the unperturbed oscillation frequency would generate a correction growing with angle if treated as a small fixed-shape perturbation. Reinterpreting it as a small frequency change captures the steadily accumulating periapsis advance instead.}
statement: The resonant part of the relativistic orbit correction shifts the radial frequency by \(3m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\).

title: Advance per radial orbit
body:
The leading extra angle is \[\Delta\varpi\simeq\frac{6\pi GM}{a(1-e^2)c^2}.\] Here \(a\) and \(e\) are the leading Keplerian semimajor axis and eccentricity. The approximation requires a weak field throughout the orbit, especially near periapsis; the advance is positive for the Schwarzschild correction.

Successive minima require the cosine argument to increase by \(2\pi\), so the angular interval is \(2\pi/(1-\delta)\simeq2\pi+2\pi\delta\). Subtracting one full revolution gives \(\Delta\varpi\simeq2\pi\delta\). Inserting \(\delta=3m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\), \(m=GM/c^2\) and \(p_{\mathrm{orb}}=a(1-e^2)\) yields the stated expression.
statement: The leading extra angle per radial orbit is \(\Delta\varpi\simeq6\pi GM/[a(1-e^2)c^2]\).

title: Separate other causes of precession
body: Other planets, a nonspherical central body and spin can also rotate the periapsis. The displayed expression isolates the test-body Schwarzschild contribution and omits radiation reaction. An exactly circular orbit has no unique periapsis direction; the nearly circular limit describes the mismatch between radial and angular frequencies.
statement: Observed periapsis motion can include perturbing bodies, nonsphericity and spin as well as the Schwarzschild correction.

title: Order corrections to slow orbital motion
body: Post-Newtonian (PN) theory extends Newtonian gravity with a controlled expansion for slow motion and a weak orbital field. It retains the nonlinear terms required at each order, unlike a calculation restricted to first order in the metric perturbation.
statement: PN theory adds consistently ordered slow-motion relativistic corrections, including necessary nonlinear metric terms.

title: Choose an order-counting parameter
body: For a gravitationally bound system define \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\coloneqq v^2/c^2\ll1\). Virial scaling makes \(GM/(rc^2)\) of the same order. Newtonian dynamics is called 0PN; relative corrections of order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\) are 1PN and 2PN. This is order counting, not an exact equality between velocity and potential for every orbit.
statement: For bound weak-field motion, PN orders count relative powers of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}=v^2/c^2\).

title: Keep a consistent collection of terms
body:
Obtaining 1PN motion generally needs \(g_{00}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\), \(g_{0i}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^{3/2}\), and spatial corrections through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) in suitable coordinates. The components enter the motion equation multiplied by different velocity factors. Keeping the same power in every component would therefore miss contributions.

\explanation{why-g00-extra}{Why retain an extra order in the time-time metric?}{A particle's metric contraction contains \(g_{00}c^2\), \(2g_{0i}cv^i\) and \(g_{ij}v^iv^j\). The last two already contain small velocity factors. Moreover, the leading constant term in the massive action describes rest energy, while the Newtonian motion comes from the next order. To correct that motion by one PN order, the time-time metric must therefore be known one order beyond its Newtonian perturbation. Keeping only linear \(h\) would miss some required contributions.}
statement: Different metric components must be kept to different orders because their contributions carry different velocity factors.

title: Conservative and dissipative corrections
body: Periapsis advance appears at 1PN. For nonspinning compact binaries, leading radiation reaction enters orbital motion at 2.5PN, relative order \((v/c)^5\), and causes secular energy loss. PN orders in a waveform or flux are counted relative to their own leading terms, so they should not be confused with orders in the acceleration.
statement: Periapsis advance is a conservative 1PN effect; leading compact-binary radiation reaction enters motion at 2.5PN.

title: Know the domain of the expansion
body: Near a merger or a horizon, slow-motion orbital expansion loses control. Widely separated compact bodies can nevertheless be treated using effective body descriptions even when their internal gravity is strong. Coordinate-dependent intermediate formulas must be compared using observables at the same retained order; more terms alone do not guarantee accuracy outside the approximation's regime. The orbital expansion describes the near zone; radiation at large distances requires matching to a wave-zone solution.
statement: PN requires slow, weak orbital interaction, but can describe widely separated bodies whose internal gravity is strong.

title: Ripples of the metric
body: Gravitational waves are propagating disturbances of spacetime geometry. In the \cref{Weak-field metric}{gr.weak_field_metric} description they are small, time-dependent metric perturbations travelling through a region that may be ordinary vacuum. They are not waves in a material medium; the geometry itself carries the changing tidal field.
statement: Gravitational waves are propagating tidal disturbances of spacetime geometry, including through vacuum.

title: Weak vacuum wave
body:
In the weak-field treatment write \(g_{\mu
u}=\eta_{\mu
u}+h_{\mu
u}\), with small components in a suitable background chart. A physical gravitational wave is a propagating perturbation with tidal curvature, rather than a coordinate ripple that can be removed by a gauge change.

Define its background trace and trace reversal by
\[ egin{aligned}h&=\eta^{\alpha eta}h_{\alpha eta},\  ar h_{\mu
u}&=h_{\mu
u}-	frac12\eta_{\mu
u}h.\end{aligned}\]
In harmonic gauge, \(\partial^\mu ar h_{\mu
u}=0\), the linear vacuum equations reduce to \(\Box ar h_{\mu
u}=0\), with \(\Box=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-
abla^2\). The constraints and gauge freedom still matter: ten independent scalar waves would overcount the physical modes.
statement: Weak vacuum gravitational radiation has non-gauge tidal curvature and satisfies a linear wave equation for its metric perturbation.

title: What the wave does
body:
A passing wave changes the relative separations of freely falling test masses transverse to its direction of travel. The observable is strain, \(h\sim\Delta L/L\), not a force pushing all objects together in the same way. This is the same tidal logic as \cref{Geodesic deviation}{gr.geodesic_deviation}, applied to a travelling curvature pattern.

\explanation{half-strain}{How does a metric perturbation change a length?}{For a transverse-traceless wave in the atlas signature, write \(H_{ij}=-h^{\mathrm{TT}}_{ij}\), so the instantaneous spatial length rule is \(d\ell^2=(\delta_{ij}+H_{ij})dx^idx^j\). For a short arm in unit direction \(n\), expansion of the square root gives \(\Delta L/L\simeq H_{ij}n^in^j/2\). This instantaneous picture assumes an arm short compared with the wavelength; a full detector response follows the light paths as well as the test masses.}
statement: Detectors measure differential tidal strain between separated freely falling masses, not a uniform push.

title: Two transverse patterns
body:
Far from sources in the transverse-traceless description, a wave travelling in one direction has two independent polarisation patterns, often called \(+\) and \(\times\). They alternately stretch and squeeze perpendicular directions. These labels describe the physical tidal pattern after gauge freedom has been fixed, not arbitrary coordinate wiggles.

Imagine a ring of initially comoving test masses perpendicular to propagation. A plus-polarised wave stretches its horizontal diameter while squeezing the vertical diameter, then reverses the roles. The cross pattern is the same stretching-and-squeezing picture rotated by 45 degrees. Their amplitudes can be combined, but a uniform expansion of the ring is not a third vacuum polarisation in GR.
statement: Two independent transverse, trace-free tidal patterns remain after gauge constraints are imposed.

title: Changing quadrupoles radiate
body: Spherical pulsation does not radiate gravitational waves in GR; a changing quadrupole-like mass distribution is the leading source. Compact binaries are the central example: their near-zone motion can be treated with \cref{Post-Newtonian approximation}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} when widely separated, while the outgoing radiation is read in the wave zone.
statement: Changing nonspherical source moments radiate; a spherically pulsating isolated source does not.

title: Not sound in space
body: Gravitational waves can pass through vacuum because they are solutions of the gravitational field equations, not pressure waves in matter. Conversely, a small coordinate ripple is not automatically a physical wave. The physical content is the gauge-invariant tidal effect that remains in detector separations.
statement: Vacuum waves are field-equation solutions, while coordinate ripples without tidal curvature need not be physical radiation.

title: An exact spherical vacuum solution
body:
The first exact solution worth learning need not begin with a black hole. Outside an ordinary spherical star there can be a vacuum region, even though the star's mass affects its geometry. With \(\Lambda=0\), that spherical vacuum geometry is Schwarzschild.

The exterior is static even if the spherical source pulsates; Birkhoff's theorem establishes this stronger result. Rotation, nonspherical radiation or an exterior electromagnetic field change the problem and require other solutions.

A black hole appears when the geometry has the appropriate extension and causal structure. The static exterior coordinates alone do not describe that extension well, so distinguish the metric solution from the limitations of the coordinates used to display it.
statement: The Schwarzschild metric is the spherical vacuum geometry with zero cosmological constant, describing more than black holes.

title: Coordinates and signature
body:
Use signature \(+---\), mass length \(m=GM/c^2\), and define
\[\begin{aligned}f(r)&=1-2m/r,\\ d\Omega^2&=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2.\end{aligned}\]
The Schwarzschild line element is
\[\begin{aligned}ds^2&=f(r)c^2dt^2-f(r)^{-1}dr^2\\ &\quad-r^2d\Omega^2.\end{aligned}\]
The time coordinate is normalised to stationary clock time at infinity, and \(r\) is the areal radius. These static exterior coordinates have \(r>2m\); the black-hole geometry can extend beyond that chart through other coordinates.
statement: With areal radius \(r\) and \(f=1-2GM/(rc^2)\), Schwarzschild has \(ds^2=fc^2dt^2-f^{-1}dr^2-r^2d\Omega^2\).

title: Deriving the spherical vacuum metric
statement: Solving the spherical vacuum radial equations and fixing asymptotic time and mass gives the Schwarzschild metric.

title: Areal radius is not radial ruler distance
body:
A symmetry sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\), which defines the geometric meaning of \(r\). Along a radial line on an exterior constant-time slice, the proper distance element is \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt{f}\). Thus coordinate radius is not generally the distance a chain of local rulers measures from a centre.

\explanation{ruler-versus-radius}{Why can circumference and radial distance disagree?}{A sphere's circumference measures \(2\pi r\), while a short radial ruler segment measures \(dr/\sqrt f\). Curvature means these relations need not assemble into the Euclidean rule “circumference equals \(2\pi\) times distance from the centre”. Moreover, a static exterior slice does not continue through the black-hole interior as a static spatial cavity.}
statement: Areal radius is defined by sphere area \(4\pi r^2\), while radial ruler length is \(dr/\sqrt f\) on a static exterior slice.

title: Read the weak-field limit
