body: At large radius, \(f=1+2\Phi/c^2\) with \(\Phi=-GM/r\), recovering the Newtonian time component. The spatial part tends to flat spherical coordinates as \(r\to\infty\). At finite radius, the exact metric retains the nonlinear geometry needed for horizons and relativistic orbit structure.
statement: The large-radius time component recovers \(\Phi=-GM/r\), while the exact metric retains strong-field effects.

title: A solution and its chart have different limits
body: An ordinary star's interior is not vacuum, so its material surface ends the exterior solution's physical applicability. For a black hole, \(r=2m\) is a failure of these coordinates; a \cref{regular extension}{gr.coordinate_singularity} crosses it. The singularity at \(r=0\) is a different, invariant problem. The static exterior description does not make the black-hole interior static.
statement: A stellar material boundary, a failed exterior chart and an invariant singularity are different limits.

title: Mass sets a length scale
body: The Schwarzschild radius translates a physical mass into a characteristic relativistic length. It locates the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole, but exists as a useful mass scale even for bodies whose surfaces lie far outside it.
statement: The length \(r_s=2GM/c^2\) is a mass scale, whether or not the body is a black hole.

title: The zero of the exterior lapse factor
body: Define \[r_s\coloneqq\frac{2GM}{c^2}=2m.\] The factor \(f(r)=1-r_s/r\) vanishes at this radius. The factors \(G\) and \(c\) convert mass to length: \([GM/c^2]=\mathrm{length}\). Doubling mass doubles the radius.
statement: The Schwarzschild radius is \(r_s=2GM/c^2=2m\), where the exterior lapse factor vanishes.

title: Compare scale with material size
body:
For \(M\simeq2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), using \(G\simeq6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) and \(c\simeq3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(r_s\simeq3.0\,\mathrm{km}\). A star of this mass can have a much larger material radius, so its exterior region never reaches this formal zero.

\explanation{solar-scale}{Check the numerical estimate}{Using the stated rounded values, \(2GM\simeq2.67\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^3s^{-2}}\), while \(c^2\simeq9.00\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\). Dividing gives about \(2.96\times10^3\,\mathrm m\). The surviving unit is metres, as required.}
statement: A solar-scale mass has Schwarzschild radius about three kilometres, much smaller than an ordinary star’s surface.

title: Compactness measures the regime
body: For material surface areal radius \(R_*\), define compactness \(\mathcal C\coloneqq GM/(R_*c^2)\). Then \(r_s/R_*=2\mathcal C\). Small compactness supports a weak-field surface treatment; approaching the Schwarzschild horizon scale requires fully relativistic reasoning and an appropriate model of the interior or collapse.
statement: Compactness \(GM/(R_*c^2)\) compares a body’s gravitational length scale with its actual surface radius.

title: Escape-speed arithmetic is only a mnemonic
body: Setting the Newtonian escape speed to \(c\) reproduces the same expression, but Newtonian mechanics cannot derive a relativistic causal boundary. The \cref{event horizon}{gr.event_horizon} is established by the metric's causal structure. For rotating or charged black holes the horizon formula changes; \(2GM/c^2\) remains a mass scale rather than their general horizon radius.
statement: Newtonian escape-speed arithmetic reproduces the length scale but cannot establish a relativistic horizon.

title: A boundary defined by escape
body:
Ask a causal question: from which events can a future-directed signal eventually reach distant observers at future null infinity? In an asymptotically flat black-hole spacetime, some events cannot. The future event horizon is the boundary separating them from events that can send a signal out.

This uses the \cref{global causal structure}{gr.causal_structure.definition}, not merely the value of one metric component. In Schwarzschild's black-hole extension the boundary sits at \(r=2m\), but the reason it is a horizon is what future light paths can do there.

An observer can cross a regular part of this boundary without meeting a material shell. Locating a general event horizon requires knowledge of the spacetime's future, so a local accelerometer cannot by itself identify it.
statement: An event horizon is a global causal escape boundary, rather than a material surface or a local curvature threshold.

title: The Schwarzschild future horizon
body:
In an asymptotically flat spacetime, the black-hole region consists of events from which no future-directed causal signal reaches future null infinity. Its boundary is the future event horizon.

In the black-hole extension of Schwarzschild, it is a null hypersurface at areal radius \(r=2m\). Its generators are light rays that remain on that boundary. Outside, some future light rays escape; inside the black-hole region, future causal paths cannot return to larger exterior radius and escape.

This definition is global. A trapped-surface or apparent-horizon criterion can provide useful local information, but is not an interchangeable definition of the event horizon.
statement: The future event horizon bounds the events that can communicate with future null infinity; in Schwarzschild it lies at \(r=2m\).

title: Use coordinates that cross the horizon
body:
Set \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\). In ingoing coordinates \(v\), the radial metric is \(ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr\), with \(f=1-2m/r\). Radial null paths obey either \(dv=0\) (ingoing) or \[\frac{dr}{dv}\overset{\text{outgoing null}}{=}\frac{f}{2}.\] The latter derivative is positive outside, zero on the horizon and negative inside. Timelike futures lie between the two null directions, so crossing inward is possible but escaping back out is not.

\explanation{future-directions}{Which way is future for the ingoing branch?}{The branch \(dv=0\) is future-directed when \(dr<0\), as fixed by the exterior time orientation. For the other branch, increasing \(v\) is future and \(dr/dv=f/2\). Inside, \(f<0\), so both future radial light directions lead to smaller \(r\). Adding angular motion cannot create a faster outward causal route. The smooth chart reveals this behaviour without treating the old coordinate divergence as a wall.}
statement: Horizon-crossing null directions show why outward escape ceases at \(r=2m\) in Schwarzschild.

title: Crossing need not be locally violent
body:
The horizon's curvature is finite, and for larger Schwarzschild mass its curvature scale is smaller. A freely falling observer crosses in finite proper time. A stationary observer held just outside instead needs proper acceleration that grows without bound towards the horizon. These are different worldlines, not conflicting descriptions of the same acceleration.

\explanation{hovering-cost}{Quantify the difference between hovering and falling}{A static observer outside Schwarzschild needs proper acceleration
\[\alpha=\frac{GM}{r^2\sqrt{1-2m/r}}.\]
As \(r\downarrow2m\), this diverges. That does not mean an infaller's accelerometer diverges: an ideal infaller has zero proper acceleration. Tidal stresses are a separate issue and can be severe for a small black hole even though horizon curvature is finite.}
statement: Free fall can cross a finite-curvature horizon, while hovering just outside requires unbounded proper acceleration.

title: A local observation cannot locate a general event horizon
body: The full future is needed to decide which events can send signals to infinity. Local trapped-surface or apparent-horizon criteria are useful but are not the definition used here. In a collapse spacetime, the event horizon need not wait for local curvature to become large. The classical causal argument does not address quantum evaporation.
statement: A general event horizon depends on the entire future causal geometry and cannot be located from local data alone.

title: A chart can fail on regular geometry
body: Divergent or degenerate-looking metric components do not by themselves establish a singular spacetime. Coordinates can cease to label events smoothly, as polar coordinates already do at the origin of a flat plane. Schwarzschild's horizon provides a physically consequential example.
statement: Metric components can fail because their coordinate chart fails, while the geometry remains regular.

title: Build a horizon-crossing chart
body:
A coordinate singularity is an apparent geometric pathology caused by a chart that does not remain regular at the suspected boundary. To establish removability, construct an extension with a smooth nondegenerate metric, rather than merely finding a few finite scalars.

For Schwarzschild, set \(c=1\), \(f=1-2m/r\), and introduce
\[\begin{aligned}r_*&=r+2m\ln\left|\frac r{2m}-1\right|,\\ v&=t+r_*.\end{aligned}\]
Since \(dr_*/dr=1/f\), we have \(dt=dv-dr/f\). Substitution gives
\[ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr-r^2d\Omega^2.\]
The divergent radial coefficient has cancelled. The resulting metric is regular across the future horizon away from angular chart axes; \(v\) here is a null coordinate, not a velocity.
statement: A coordinate singularity is a removable chart failure; ingoing coordinates remove Schwarzschild’s horizon divergence.

title: Check nondegeneracy as well as finiteness
body: The radial components are \(g_{vv}=f\), \(g_{vr}=g_{rv}=-1\), and \(g_{rr}=0\). Their two-dimensional determinant is \(f\cdot0-(-1)^2=-1\), including at \(r=2m\). Thus the metric remains nondegenerate and Lorentzian there. The full determinant is \(-r^4\sin^2\theta\); polar-axis zeros are the familiar angular chart issue.
statement: The ingoing radial metric has determinant \(-1\), so it remains nondegenerate at the horizon.

title: An extension, not a regular old chart
body: The transformation is smooth on its overlap with the exterior chart but singular at that chart's boundary. The resulting ingoing metric extends smoothly across the future horizon, admitting finite tangent components for infalling paths. This demonstrates regularity more strongly than checking a few finite curvature scalars alone.
statement: The new chart extends the geometry across a boundary of the old chart; the transformation need not be regular at that old boundary.

title: Coordinates cannot remove every singularity
body: At \(r=0\), the Schwarzschild Kretschmann scalar diverges, so no smooth chart change can make the classical curvature regular. Conversely, finite invariants alone are not a universal proof of extendibility. Distinguish chart failure, invariant curvature behaviour and geodesic completeness when diagnosing an apparent boundary.
statement: Chart extension, invariant curvature and geodesic completeness are separate diagnostic questions.

title: The Schwarzschild interior reaches a geometric boundary
body: In the black-hole region of the classical Schwarzschild solution, decreasing areal radius is unavoidable along future causal motion. The boundary \(r=0\) is a spacelike singularity, not a material point waiting somewhere inside a static spatial cavity.
statement: The Schwarzschild black-hole interior ends at a spacelike singular boundary, not a regular central point in a static cavity.

title: Invariant curvature diverges
body:
After removable chart boundaries have been extended where possible, a classical singularity is diagnosed by an inextendible causal geodesic with finite proper time or affine length. The singularity need not be an ordinary event in the manifold, and this criterion does not require every singular geometry to have divergent scalar invariants.

In Schwarzschild's black-hole region, \(r\to0\) is a spacelike singular boundary. With \(m=GM/c^2\), its Kretschmann scalar is
\[K=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=48m^2/r^6.\]
This diverges as \(r\to0\), while remaining finite at the horizon \(r=2m\). A regular coordinate change cannot remove the divergent scalar. Schwarzschild therefore exhibits both geodesic incompleteness and invariant curvature growth.
statement: The classical Schwarzschild singularity has divergent invariant curvature and incomplete causal geodesics at \(r\to0\).

title: A falling observer has finite remaining time
body:
Consider the ideal radial geodesic released from rest at infinity. Its dimensionless conserved energy is one. The exact radial normalisation gives
\[\frac{dr}{d\tau}=-c\sqrt{2m/r},\]
where the negative sign selects inward motion. Thus the remaining proper time from the horizon is
\[\begin{aligned}\Delta\tau&=\frac1c\int_0^{2m}\sqrt{\frac r{2m}}\,dr\\ &=\frac{4m}{3c}.\end{aligned}\]
The integrand tends to zero towards \(r=0\), so the proper-time integral converges even though curvature diverges. This is not a universal lifetime for every interior observer: other initial energies give other values. Nor does the calculation continue the geodesic through the singular boundary.
statement: For radial free fall from rest at infinity, horizon-to-singularity proper time is \(4m/(3c)\).

title: Singularity means incomplete classical geometry
body: The singular boundary is not a regular event belonging to the spacetime manifold. In the general theory, singularity statements concern inextendible causal geodesics of finite affine length or proper time; they need not always involve divergent scalar invariants. Schwarzschild has both finite-time incompleteness and divergent curvature.
statement: Singularity theorems concern incomplete classical geometry, rather than necessarily an infinite scalar at a regular event.

title: Do not turn breakdown into a microscopic model
body: Classical GR gives no regular matter state at this boundary or account of what replaces it. Quantum gravity may be needed, but a particular resolution is not supplied by the solution. The Schwarzschild spacelike singularity also should not be copied unchanged into rotating or charged black-hole geometries.
statement: Classical breakdown does not provide a microscopic state or a specific quantum-gravity resolution.

title: Use symmetry to reduce radial motion
body:
A particle orbit involves several changing coordinates, but symmetry removes much of the work. Time independence supplies a conserved energy parameter, and rotational symmetry supplies angular momentum. The orbital plane can then be chosen as the equatorial plane.

Insert those constants into the tangent's norm. What remains is a radial equation resembling a one-dimensional energy balance. Its effective potential reveals turning points, circular orbits and stability without solving the entire trajectory first.

This combines the \cref{Schwarzschild metric}{gr.schwarzschild_metric.definition} with geodesic motion and the metric normalisation. The potential is a useful algebraic organisation of the same geometry, not an additional gravitational field or an ordinary material energy density.
statement: Schwarzschild symmetries reduce geodesic motion to a one-dimensional radial equation with conserved parameters.

title: Fix the energy normalisation
body:
Use \(c=1\), mass length \(m=GM/c^2\), \(f=1-2m/r\) and equatorial motion. For a timelike geodesic parametrised by proper time, define
\[\begin{aligned}\mathcal E&=f\dot t,\\ L&=r^2\dot\phi,\\ V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)&=f\left(1+\frac{L^2}{r^2}\right).\end{aligned}\]
Both \(\mathcal E\) and \(L\) are constants. The radial equation is \(\dot r^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal E^2\). Here \(\mathcal E\) is energy per unit rest energy and \(L\) is specific angular momentum in the announced geometric units; dots denote proper-time derivatives.

At fixed \(L\), allowed radii have \(\mathcal E^2\geq V_{\mathrm{eff}}\). Equality gives a radial turning point. The potential depends on the particle's angular momentum and causal type, so it is not one universal function for every path.
statement: In natural units, timelike radial motion obeys \(\dot r^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal E^2\), with \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}=(1-2m/r)(1+L^2/r^2)\).

title: Insert the constants into the norm
body:
For equatorial Schwarzschild geodesics in \(c=1\) units, the quadratic path Lagrangian is
\[2\mathcal L=f\dot t^2-f^{-1}\dot r^2-r^2\dot\phi^2.\]
Because \(t\) and \(\phi\) do not appear explicitly, their Euler–Lagrange equations give constants \(f\dot t=\mathcal E\) and \(r^2\dot\phi=L\) (the conjugate angular momentum has the opposite sign in this metric convention; \(L\) is defined as written).

Now impose the timelike norm \(2\mathcal L=1\) and multiply by \(f\):
\[\begin{aligned}f&=\mathcal E^2-\dot r^2-fL^2/r^2,\\ \dot r^2+f(1+L^2/r^2)&=\mathcal E^2.\end{aligned}\]
Thus the metric symmetries and the norm together give the radial reduction. At a turning point \(\dot r=0\), but a circular orbit also requires zero radial acceleration, so a second condition is needed.
statement: Substituting symmetry constants into the timelike norm produces the radial effective-potential equation.

title: Circular orbits and stability
body:
A circular orbit needs both \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal E^2\) and \(V'_{\mathrm{eff}}=0\) at fixed \(L\). The latter gives \(L^2=mr^2/(r-3m)\). The outer minimum is stable for \(r>6m\); the inner maximum is unstable for \(3m<r<6m\). The limiting orbit at \(r=6m\) is marginally stable, the ISCO. A turning point alone is not a circular orbit.

\explanation{stability-derivatives}{Check the stability criterion}{At fixed \(L\), expand \(V=1-2m/r+L^2/r^2-2mL^2/r^3\). The circular condition \(V'=0\) gives \(L^2=mr^2/(r-3m)\), requiring \(r>3m\). Differentiate a second time before substituting this relation. At the circular radius,
\[V''=\frac{2m(r-6m)}{r^3(r-3m)}.\]
It is positive at a minimum for \(r>6m\), negative at a maximum for \(3m<r<6m\), and zero at \(6m\). Differentiating after substituting a radius-dependent \(L\) would incorrectly vary the conserved angular momentum during the stability test.}
statement: Timelike circular orbits are stable for \(r>6m\), unstable for \(3m<r<6m\), and marginal at the ISCO \(r=6m\).

title: Null geodesics have a different potential
body: For an affine parameter \(\lambda\), define the analogous constants \(\mathcal E=f\,dt/d\lambda\) and \(L=r^2d\phi/d\lambda\). Zero tangent norm gives \(V_{\mathrm{null}}=fL^2/r^2\) and \((dr/d\lambda)^2+V_{\mathrm{null}}=\mathcal E^2\). This potential has a maximum at \(r=3m\), the unstable photon sphere. Null constants change under affine rescaling, but \(b\coloneqq L/\mathcal E\), the asymptotic impact parameter, does not.
statement: The null potential has an unstable maximum at \(r=3m\); null energy and angular momentum share an affine scaling freedom.

title: Einstein's happiest thought
body: In 1907 Einstein realised that an observer falling freely from a roof would not feel their own weight. He later called this insight the happiest thought of his life. The equivalence between free fall and inertial motion gave him a physical route beyond special relativity: gravity might be removed locally by choosing the right state of motion.
statement: Einstein’s 1907 free-fall insight suggested that gravitational effects could disappear locally.

title: From Galileo to Eötvös
body: The empirical seed was the universality of free fall: different bodies accelerate alike when non-gravitational effects are removed. Newton encoded the same fact as equality of inertial and gravitational mass, while Eötvös and later experiments tested that equality with increasing precision. Einstein promoted this numerical coincidence into a principle about all local non-gravitational physics.
statement: Universality of free fall supplied the experimental starting point for Einstein’s broader principle.

title: Why gravity became geometry
body: Einstein's equivalence principle suggested that gravitational acceleration could disappear in a freely falling laboratory, but tidal differences between neighbouring laboratories could not. Riemann's mathematics supplied a language in which geometry is locally flat yet globally curved. By 1915 Einstein had identified the gravitational field with spacetime geometry rather than a force acting within a fixed Euclidean arena.
statement: Einstein combined local free-fall physics with Riemann’s curved geometry in the path to GR.

title: Einstein and Grossmann
body: Einstein did not reach the geometric theory alone. His friend Marcel Grossmann guided him toward the tensor calculus developed by Riemann, Christoffel, Ricci and Levi-Civita, and their 1913 Entwurf theory was an important but incomplete step. The collaboration illustrates how a physical principle and an existing mathematical language had to be brought together before the final field equations were possible.
statement: Grossmann helped connect Einstein’s physical ideas to the existing mathematics of tensor geometry.

title: From Riemann's line element to a gravitational field
body: Riemann's 1854 lecture generalised geometry by allowing the coefficients of a quadratic line element to vary from point to point. Einstein turned that measuring structure into physics: the metric determines clock rates, spatial measurements and light cones while also responding to matter. What had been geometrical data became a dynamical gravitational field.
statement: Riemann’s variable measuring geometry became a dynamical gravitational field in Einstein’s theory.

title: From light cones to global causality
body: Minkowski made light cones central to special-relativistic geometry, but curved spacetime allowed their orientation to vary from event to event. Mid-twentieth-century work by Gödel, Penrose, Hawking and others showed that the global arrangement of cones controls horizons, closed causal curves and singularity theorems. Causality thereby became a subject in its own right rather than a local side-effect of the metric.
statement: Twentieth-century relativity made the global arrangement of light cones central to horizons and causality.

title: Connecting neighbouring tangent spaces
body: Ordinary derivatives silently compare vectors at different points as though all directions belonged to one fixed vector space. Nineteenth-century differential geometry exposed the limitation, and Weyl and Cartan developed the modern idea of an affine connection in the early twentieth century. A connection makes the comparison rule explicit and can therefore describe geometry even before a metric is chosen.
statement: The connection made comparison between neighbouring vector spaces an explicit geometric rule.

title: Christoffel's differential forms
body: Elwin Bruno Christoffel introduced the quantities now called Christoffel symbols in an 1869 study of quadratic differential forms. They were not initially components of a gravitational field; they organised how derivatives change under a change of coordinates. In general relativity the same bookkeeping quantities encode the metric connection, while their ability to vanish at one point warns that they are not themselves curvature.
statement: Christoffel’s 1869 quantities organised differentiation under changes of coordinates before their use in GR.

title: The absolute differential calculus
body: Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro developed methods of invariant differentiation during the late nineteenth century, and with Tullio Levi-Civita presented the absolute differential calculus systematically in 1900. Einstein and Grossmann adopted this machinery because ordinary component derivatives do not transform tensorially in curved coordinates. The covariant derivative became the device that lets local equations retain geometric meaning.
statement: Ricci and Levi-Civita’s calculus supplied derivatives that retain geometric meaning across coordinates.

title: Levi-Civita's distinguished connection
body: For a metric geometry there is a unique connection that preserves the metric and has no torsion: the connection now named for Levi-Civita. Cartan later made torsion an independent geometric object, showing that its absence is a physical and geometric choice rather than part of the definition of every connection. Standard general relativity makes that torsion-free choice.
statement: Cartan distinguished torsion from curvature, making the torsion-free GR choice explicit.

title: Levi-Civita invents parallel transport
body: In 1917 Levi-Civita gave an intrinsic rule for carrying a direction along a curve on a general Riemannian manifold. The construction replaced an ambient-space picture of parallel arrows with one defined entirely inside the geometry. Its path dependence provided an immediate geometric interpretation of curvature and soon became part of the working language of relativity.
statement: Levi-Civita’s intrinsic transport rule gave curvature a direct path-comparison interpretation.

title: From shortest routes to free fall
body: Geodesics began as the shortest or straightest curves on surfaces, studied in geodesy and differential geometry. General relativity changed their physical status: a freely falling test body follows a timelike geodesic, while light follows null geodesics. Gravity was thus shifted from a force bending a trajectory to the geometry that defines what unforced motion means.
statement: GR identified geometrically unforced timelike and null paths with physical free fall and light propagation.

title: Riemann makes curvature intrinsic
body: In his 1854 habilitation lecture Riemann proposed that geometry could vary from place to place and in dimensions beyond ordinary surfaces. The curvature tensor bearing his name packages the obstruction to treating that geometry as flat. Einstein's theory made this abstract nineteenth-century construction observable through tidal gravity and geodesic deviation.
statement: Riemann made curvature intrinsic; GR made that structure observable through tides and free fall.

title: Ricci's contraction enters physics
body: The contracted curvature tensor is named for Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro, whose invariant calculus helped organise the geometry inherited by general relativity. Einstein spent years testing curvature combinations that could represent gravitation and source equations. The Ricci tensor became decisive because vacuum gravity can set it to zero while leaving the full Riemann curvature—and therefore tidal gravity—nonzero.
statement: Ricci’s contracted curvature became central to equations that permit curved vacuum outside matter.

title: The trace term that closes the equation
body: Einstein's route to the final field equations repeatedly approached the Ricci tensor but struggled with covariance and conservation. In November 1915 the trace-adjusted combination now called the Einstein tensor supplied the required divergence-free left-hand side. The extra scalar-curvature term is therefore not cosmetic: it is what lets geometry match local stress-energy conservation.
statement: Einstein’s trace-adjusted curvature combination reconciled the field equation with local source consistency.

title: An old identity gains physical force
body: The differential identities bearing Luigi Bianchi's name arose in nineteenth-century geometry, before general relativity. Their contraction implies that the Einstein tensor has zero covariant divergence. Once Einstein's equations tied that tensor to matter, a geometric identity became the consistency condition behind covariant stress-energy conservation.
statement: Bianchi’s geometric identities later supplied the consistency relation for Einstein’s matter coupling.

title: Separating geometry from coordinates
body: Relativity's freedom to change coordinates made component divergences an unreliable guide to physical singularities. Scalar contractions of curvature supplied coordinate-independent tests, with the invariant associated with Erich Kretschmann becoming especially familiar in the Schwarzschild geometry. Such invariants helped distinguish the removable pathology at the horizon from genuine curvature growth at the centre.
statement: Curvature invariants helped separate the Schwarzschild horizon’s chart problem from genuine central curvature growth.

title: Einstein, Hilbert and the action
body: David Hilbert presented a variational formulation of gravitation in late 1915 while Einstein was completing the field equations by a different route. Their work was closely timed and historically entangled, but the modern Einstein-Hilbert action should not be read as evidence that one simply supplied the other's theory. Its enduring importance is structural: one scalar action yields the geometric field equations and makes extensions of GR systematic.
statement: Hilbert’s variational formulation and Einstein’s field-equation work converged in late 1915 through distinct routes.

title: Assumptions built for global theorems
body: Energy conditions were developed as deliberately broad inequalities rather than detailed models of matter. Raychaudhuri's focusing equation and the singularity theorems of Penrose and Hawking used them to turn local curvature assumptions into global conclusions. Quantum fields can violate several classical energy conditions, so their historical success does not make them inviolable laws of nature.
statement: Energy conditions let focusing and singularity theorems state broad, explicit matter hypotheses.

title: Four weeks in November 1915
body: Einstein presented a sequence of communications to the Prussian Academy in November 1915, revising the gravitational equations almost weekly. On 25 November he gave the generally covariant equations in essentially their modern form. The compressed chronology hides an eight-year search through equivalence, covariance, conservation and the Newtonian limit.
statement: Einstein’s November 1915 communications culminated in the generally covariant field equations.

title: Einstein and Hilbert
body: Hilbert submitted an action-based treatment of gravitation within days of Einstein's final academy paper. The surviving record supports independent but interacting routes rather than a simple tale of theft or solitary discovery. Einstein supplied the sustained physical programme and final tensor equation; Hilbert's variational formulation revealed a powerful mathematical organisation of the same theory.
statement: Einstein’s physical programme and Hilbert’s variational route were independent but interacting contributions.

title: Einstein's static universe
body: Einstein introduced the cosmological term in 1917 when applying general relativity to the universe as a whole. He sought a spatially closed, static model, reflecting the limited astronomical evidence then available; without the added term his chosen matter distribution would not remain static. The construction also helped found relativistic cosmology, even though the equilibrium was unstable.
statement: Einstein introduced the term in 1917 to obtain a static cosmological model.

title: From discarded term to dark energy
body: After expanding-universe models and observations displaced the static universe, Einstein no longer favoured his original motivation for the term. The cosmological constant nevertheless remained mathematically legitimate and acquired new interpretations as vacuum energy or dark energy. The discovery of accelerated cosmic expansion in the late 1990s returned it to the centre of cosmology.
statement: Accelerated cosmic expansion revived the cosmological constant’s importance after its original static motivation was abandoned.

title: Einstein predicts gravitational clock shifts
body: Einstein used the equivalence principle in 1907 to argue that gravity must affect clock rates and light frequency. A uniformly accelerating laboratory supplied the thought experiment: light received higher or lower in the cabin has a shifted frequency because the receiver changes velocity during the signal's flight. Reinterpreting acceleration as gravity produced one of the theory's earliest testable consequences.
statement: Einstein inferred gravitational clock shifts from an accelerating-laboratory argument in 1907.

title: Pound and Rebka measure the shift
body: In 1959–60 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka used the Mössbauer effect to compare gamma rays over the height of Harvard's Jefferson tower. The expected terrestrial shift was extraordinarily small, but recoil-free nuclear resonance made it measurable. Their result turned a once-astronomical relativistic effect into a laboratory measurement and anticipated today's gravitational corrections to precision clocks.
statement: Pound and Rebka used nuclear resonance to measure the tiny terrestrial gravitational frequency shift.

title: From the equivalence principle to the full prediction
body: Einstein predicted solar light bending in 1911 using the equivalence principle, obtaining only half the value of the completed theory. The 1915 field equations added the effect of spatial curvature and doubled the prediction to about 1.75 arcseconds for a ray grazing the Sun. The change is a useful historical warning: equivalence gives local insight but not the complete spacetime geometry.
statement: The completed theory doubled Einstein’s earlier half-value prediction by including the spatial metric contribution.

title: The 1919 eclipse expeditions
body: British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington and Andrew Crommelin photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun in 1919. Their reported deflections favoured Einstein's prediction and made both Einstein and general relativity internationally famous. The measurements were difficult and less decisive than the legend sometimes suggests, but later radio and lensing observations confirmed the relativistic effect with far greater precision.
statement: The 1919 eclipse expeditions favoured Einstein’s bending prediction; later observations tested it much more precisely.

title: Mercury's unexplained 43 arcseconds
body: Urbain Le Verrier showed in the nineteenth century that known Newtonian perturbations left a small residual advance of Mercury's perihelion. Proposed planets and modifications of gravity failed to settle the anomaly. In November 1915 Einstein obtained the remaining roughly 43 arcseconds per century from his new theory, a result that he regarded as a decisive personal triumph.
statement: Einstein explained Mercury’s residual advance of roughly 43 arcseconds per century in November 1915.

title: Einstein's wave prediction
body: Einstein found wave-like weak-field solutions in 1916 and corrected the energy-emission formula in 1918, producing the quadrupole pattern characteristic of gravity. Because coordinate freedom can manufacture apparent ripples, even Einstein later became uncertain about whether exact waves were physical. The episode showed how difficult it was to separate gravitational radiation from coordinate artefacts.
statement: Einstein’s weak-field calculations predicted radiation, while coordinate freedom complicated its early interpretation.

title: Do gravitational waves carry energy?
body: Work by Bondi, Pirani, Robinson and others in the 1950s clarified invariant effects and energy transport by gravitational waves. Feynman's “sticky bead” argument gave a memorable operational test: a passing wave can do work by making beads slide and heat a rod. The reality question was thereby reframed in terms of measurable tidal effects rather than troublesome coordinate components.
statement: Tidal work and asymptotic energy balance clarified that gravitational radiation has measurable physical effects.

title: GW150914
body: On 14 September 2015 the two Advanced LIGO detectors recorded GW150914, a signal from merging stellar-mass black holes. Its evolving waveform matched general-relativistic calculations through inspiral, merger and ringdown. Announced in 2016, it was the first direct detection of gravitational waves and opened gravitational-wave astronomy.
statement: GW150914 provided the first direct gravitational-wave detection, from a binary black-hole merger.

title: Schwarzschild's wartime solution
body: Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact solution of Einstein's field equations only weeks after their final publication, while serving on the Russian front during the First World War. Einstein presented the paper to the Prussian Academy in January 1916. The solution's apparent singular surface later became central to black-hole physics, although that interpretation was not available to Schwarzschild himself.
statement: Schwarzschild found the first exact GR field solution within weeks of Einstein’s final 1915 equations.

title: The surface that stopped being singular
body: The radius now called the horizon looked singular in standard Schwarzschild coordinates, encouraging decades of uncertainty about whether it was a physical barrier. Horizon-crossing coordinates developed through work by Eddington, Lemaître and Finkelstein showed that regular infall continues across it. The suspect surface was reinterpreted as a one-way causal boundary rather than a place of divergent curvature.
statement: Regular infalling coordinates turned a suspected singular barrier into a one-way causal boundary.

title: From collapsed stars to black holes
body: Oppenheimer and Snyder modelled continuing stellar collapse in 1939, but relativistic collapsed objects remained marginal for decades. Global causal methods in the 1960s made horizons and trapped surfaces precise, while John Wheeler helped popularise the term “black hole”. The event horizon is the mature geometric concept behind that name, defined by which signals can ever escape.
statement: Collapse models and global causal methods made the modern black-hole region precise.

title: Coordinates created a false obstruction
body: Early discussion often treated the Schwarzschild radius as a singular edge because the original static coordinates fail there. Lemaître's freely falling coordinates and later Eddington-Finkelstein and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates crossed the surface smoothly. The episode became the standard lesson that divergent metric components diagnose a chart only after invariant geometry has been checked.
statement: Horizon-crossing coordinate systems resolved the false obstruction in the original static Schwarzschild chart.

title: From ideal collapse to singularity theorems
body: Oppenheimer and Snyder's 1939 model showed that sufficiently massive idealised matter could collapse beyond its Schwarzschild radius, but symmetry left open whether the singular outcome was an artefact. Penrose's 1965 theorem used trapped surfaces and global causality to show that geodesic incompleteness is a robust prediction under broad conditions. Singularity became a statement about the limits of classical spacetime, not merely an infinite number in special coordinates.
statement: Penrose’s theorem showed that geodesic incompleteness need not be an artefact of perfectly symmetric collapse.

title: Causal structure — visual model
body: The cones partition causal futures, pasts, and spacelike separation.
statement: Future and past cones meet at one event.

title: Equivalence principle — visual model
body: Acceleration and uniform gravity have the same local experimental signature; tidal effects are deliberately excluded from this small-lab picture.
statement: Two local laboratories show the same ball behaviour under a and g.

title: Freely falling observer — visual model
body: Free fall is inertial motion in GR; the supported observer cue shows what free fall is not.
statement: The observer follows a blue free-fall path without thrust.

title: Gravity as geometry — visual model
body: The detail graphic contrasts force-on-background intuition with GR's geometric view: free motion follows spacetime geometry.
statement: A gold free path follows the curved spacetime geometry.

title: Inverse metric — visual model
body: The inverse metric reverses metric contraction and raises indices.
statement: Metric and inverse tiles contract to delta.

title: Line element — visual model
body: The metric turns coordinate displacement into invariant interval.
statement: A gold ds-squared segment joins nearby events.

title: Local flatness — visual model
body: Curved spacetime is locally Minkowskian at a chosen event.
statement: A small flat frame sits within a curved patch.

title: Local inertial frame — visual model
body: SR is recovered locally: near one event the curved geometry has a small flat frame with x and ct axes.
statement: A small x-ct frame sits on a local flat patch of curved spacetime.

title: Metric signature convention — visual model
body: Either signature works when definitions and calculations remain consistent.
statement: Two signature tiles present the standard alternatives.

title: Spacetime metric — visual model
body: The metric determines spacetime lengths, times, angles, and causal intervals.
statement: A g glyph sits on curved spacetime geometry.

title: Null curve — visual model
body: Null motion lies exactly on the causal cone with ds-squared zero.
statement: A gold light path follows the cone boundary.

title: Proper time in curved spacetime — visual model

title: Build the tensor from rest-frame isotropy
body:
Given a fluid four-velocity \(u\), its rest frame has no preferred spatial direction. A symmetric tensor formed only from \(u\), the metric and scalar fluid properties must therefore have the form
\[T^{\mu\nu}=A u^\mu u^\nu+B g^{\mu\nu}.\]
In that frame \(u^{\hat\mu}=(c,0,0,0)\). The spatial diagonal entries are \(-B\), so the measured pressure requires \(B=-p\). The time-time entry is then \(Ac^2-p\); setting it equal to the measured energy density \(\epsilon\) gives \(A=(\epsilon+p)/c^2\).

Thus isotropic \cref{stress-energy measurements}{gr.stress_energy_tensor.authored_3}, the \cref{normalised fluid tangent}{gr.four_velocity.definition} and the metric combine to determine the tensor. Additional heat flow or anisotropic stress would require additional tensor structures.
statement: Rest-frame density and isotropic pressure fix the coefficients of \(u^\mu u^\nu\) and \(g^{\mu\nu}\).

title: Combine gravitational and matter responses
body:
Use natural units \(c=1\), \(\kappa=8\pi G\), and the atlas sign conventions. The \cref{gravitational variation}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action.authored_3} gives a coefficient \(-(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u})/(2\kappa)\). Define the matter source by its metric response, \(\delta S_m=	frac12\int dV_4\,T_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}\).

For compactly supported interior variations, the total first variation is
\[\delta S=	frac12\int dV_4\,C_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u},\]
where
\[C_{\mu
u}=- rac{G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}}{\kappa}+T_{\mu
u}.\]
Requiring \(\delta S=0\) for every symmetric interior variation sets \(C_{\mu
u}=0\). This yields Einstein's field equation. Restoring dimensions gives \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\).

This derivation combines a chosen gravitational action with the definition of matter response. Its conclusion is conditional on that action and the boundary treatment; a different curvature action can give different field equations.
statement: Stationarity of the chosen total action equates its geometric and matter metric-response coefficients.

title: From zero source to Ricci flatness
body:
Given Einstein's equation, set \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\) and \(\Lambda=0\). Then \(R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu}=0\). Trace it with the inverse metric in four dimensions:
\[0=R-\tfrac12(4)R=-R.\]
So \(R=0\), and substituting back gives \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\). Conversely, Ricci flatness sets both terms to zero and satisfies the vacuum equation.

This argument combines the source-free field equation with a contraction of Ricci. It does not set the full Riemann tensor to zero; the uncontracted tidal information can remain.
statement: The vacuum trace sets \(R=0\), leaving \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) when \(\Lambda=0\).

title: The weak, slow and nearly static regime
body:
The Newtonian limit of GR is the approximation in which \(|\Phi|/c^2\ll1\), test bodies and sources move slowly compared with light, source pressure is small compared with rest energy density, and the gravitational field changes slowly on the time scale of the experiment. Set \(\Lambda=0\) or neglect its effects on the region being studied.

Under these assumptions, the geodesic equation becomes \(d^2\mathbf x/dt^2=-\nabla\Phi\), while Einstein's equation becomes \(\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho\). Both are needed: the first tells matter how to move in a given potential, and the second tells the potential how to respond to mass density.
statement: The Newtonian limit uses small potentials, slow matter and test bodies, low pressure and negligible time variation.

title: An orbit whose closest approach advances
body:
A bound orbit reaches a minimum radius once per radial cycle. If successive minima occur at angular separation \(2\pi+\Delta\varpi\), then \(\Delta\varpi\) is its periapsis advance; “perihelion” refers specifically to an orbit about the Sun.

For a weak-field test-body orbit about a spherical nonrotating mass with \(\Lambda=0\), the leading GR contribution is \(\Delta\varpi\simeq6\pi GM/[a(1-e^2)c^2]\). Here \(a\) and \(e\) describe the leading Keplerian ellipse. This isolates the Schwarzschild effect from precession caused by other bodies, nonsphericity or spin.
statement: Perihelion precession is the extra angular revolution between successive closest approaches in a bound orbit.

title: From vacuum curvature to a wave equation
body:
Use the weak-field metric split, raise perturbation indices with \(\eta\), and retain only terms linear in \(h\). The connection is first order, so the Ricci calculation keeps its derivatives and drops its quadratic products.

Introduce harmonic gauge \(\partial^\mu ar h_{\mu
u}=0\). Since \( ar h_{\mu
u}=h_{\mu
u}-\eta_{\mu
u}h/2\), this says \(\partial^\mu h_{\mu
u}=\partial_
u h/2\). In Ricci, the resulting mixed second derivatives cancel, leaving
\[R^{(1)}_{\mu
u}=-	frac12\Box h_{\mu
u}.\]
Taking the trace and forming \(G^{(1)}_{\mu
u}=R^{(1)}_{\mu
u}-\eta_{\mu
u}R^{(1)}/2\) gives
\[G^{(1)}_{\mu
u}=-	frac12\Box ar h_{\mu
u}.\]
The vacuum field equation with \(\Lambda=0\) sets this to zero. Thus the weak metric supplies the expansion, trace adjustment isolates the useful variable, and the vacuum equation supplies propagation. Exact nonlinear waves require more than this approximation.
statement: The harmonic condition reduces the first-order Einstein tensor to \(-\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu}/2\).

title: Cancel the divergent radial term
body:
In natural units the Schwarzschild radial metric is \(ds^2_{\mathrm{rad}}=fdt^2-f^{-1}dr^2\). Insert the ingoing coordinate relation:
\[\begin{aligned}fdt^2&=f(dv-dr/f)^2\\ &=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr+dr^2/f.\end{aligned}\]
Subtracting the old radial term removes the last contribution, leaving \(ds^2_{\mathrm{rad}}=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr\). Nothing has been approximated.

Its radial metric matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}f&-1\\ -1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with determinant \(-1\) even at \(f=0\). So finite coefficients also form a nondegenerate Lorentzian metric. This is the constructive check that the horizon is not a curvature singularity.
statement: Substituting \(dt=dv-dr/f\) cancels the \(dr^2/f\) terms exactly.

title: The critical impact parameter for photon capture
body:
Use natural units and the affine null radial equation \(\dot r^2+fL^2/r^2=\mathcal E^2\). For a nonradial ray from infinity, \(b=L/\mathcal E\) is its asymptotic impact parameter. Although both constants change under rescaling the affine parameter, their ratio does not.

The null potential has its maximum at \(r=3m\), where \(f=1/3\). Its height is \(L^2/(27m^2)\). The limiting incoming ray just matches that height:
\[\mathcal E^2=\frac{L^2}{27m^2},\qquad |b|=3\sqrt3\,m.\]
Smaller impact magnitudes pass over the barrier and are captured; larger ones have an outer turning point and scatter back out. The critical ideal ray asymptotically approaches the unstable circular photon orbit. This is a strong-field result, beyond the leading weak-deflection formula.
statement: For incoming Schwarzschild light rays, the unstable photon sphere gives \(b_{\mathrm{crit}}=3\sqrt3\,m\).
